glossary.entries.attention.body.0: A convolution only looks at a small ring around itself, so when the clue is at the far side of the image it takes many layers to reach it. Self-attention lets every position compare itself with every other in one step: the image is cut into patches, each called a token, and each scores every patch by how alike they are, then takes an average weighted by those scores.
glossary.entries.attention.body.1: In detail, each patch has a query q, a key k and a value v: the score is q·k/√d, softmax turns the scores into weights that add up to 1, and the v of every patch are averaged with those weights. ViT, from 2020, handles images this way.
glossary.entries.attention.title: Self-attention
glossary.entries.autoencoder.body.0: An squeezes a whole image into a few numbers z, and a draws an image back from z; the training target is the input itself, so no labels are needed. Such a pair is called an autoencoder.
glossary.entries.autoencoder.body.1: The narrowest layer in the middle is the bottleneck. It needs at least as many numbers as the ways the images really vary: a family of images that varies only left–right and up–down needs at least two numbers, since one number can only move along a single line.
glossary.entries.autoencoder.body.2: Compression and denoising both start from this step.
glossary.entries.autoencoder.title: Autoencoders and the bottleneck
glossary.entries.bench.body.0: Not every level is a circuit. A bench is a figure you can work with your hands: drag things, turn knobs, push sliders, and the figure changes at once, showing live whether the goals are met.
glossary.entries.bench.body.1: One kind of bench holds just a black box: pick test pictures to feed in, compare what goes in with what comes out, then say what it did. Experimenting before concluding is the most reliable way to get to know an unfamiliar tool.
glossary.entries.bench.title: Benches
glossary.entries.bgsub.body.0: A turns shades of grey into “yes” or “no”: cells above it become 1 and the rest 0. An image of only 0s and 1s is called a mask, and it marks out a region of the picture.
glossary.entries.bgsub.body.1: For a fixed camera looking for whatever comes into view, comparing with a reference shot of the empty scene works far better than looking for bright spots: wherever the difference is large is new. This is background subtraction, and it sidesteps the unknown of how bright things were to begin with.
glossary.entries.bgsub.body.2: A threshold is the simplest kind of decision, and the most fragile: the result depends entirely on where the threshold sits, and a fixed threshold often fails once the lighting changes.
glossary.entries.bgsub.title: Thresholds, masks and background subtraction
glossary.entries.channels.body.0: A colour image is three images stacked together, one each for red, green and blue, called three channels. Each layer of a convolutional network usually outputs many channels too, one per filter.
glossary.entries.channels.body.1: A convolution kernel has to cover all the input channels at once: a 3×3 kernel over 3 channels has 3×3×3 = 27 weights, and the three sets of products add up to one output. The weights for different channels can have opposite signs, so whatever brightens in every channel cancels out and only the colour contrast is left.
glossary.entries.channels.body.2: In the first layer of a trained convolutional network you often find such filters tuned to colour contrast: red against green and blue against yellow, the same two colour oppositions as in the human retina.
glossary.entries.channels.title: Multiple channels
glossary.entries.circuit.body.0: Most levels ask you to build a circuit. The “Input” part holds the data the level gives you and the “Output” part is the result you hand in; each part also says whether it carries an image, a waveform or a number. In between you place parts and wire them together.
glossary.entries.circuit.body.1: Every part has one or more input ports (such as a and b, or left and right) and a single output dot. A wire runs from one block’s output dot to another block’s input port: an output can feed many places, but each input port reads from one wire. Wires cannot form a loop, since a block cannot wait for itself to finish.
glossary.entries.circuit.body.2: Some parts have settings: what to multiply by, how high a threshold is, which way to shift, nine weights. Change a setting and the results on every part update at once; a part with an input left unwired says it is missing one.
glossary.entries.circuit.body.3: Every part shows what it produces on the currently selected test, so you can follow the image as it changes along the circuit.
glossary.entries.circuit.title: Building a circuit
glossary.entries.cnn.body.0: A convolutional neural network (CNN) strings these pieces together: convolutions find local strokes and textures, ReLU separates “there” from “not there”, pooling shrinks the image and tolerates shifts, and finally a dense layer and a sigmoid turn the features into a score. A task that answers “what is this?” is called classification.
glossary.entries.cnn.body.1: The kernels in the network are not designed by anyone but learned from examples: the weights start as small random numbers and training turns them into useful features. In most vision tasks, learned features have replaced hand-designed ones.
glossary.entries.cnn.body.2: If every operation along the way were linear, the whole network would amount to a single linear operation, and many simple distinctions would be out of reach.
glossary.entries.cnn.title: Convolutional neural networks
glossary.entries.colour.body.0: Real light is a whole spectrum: so much of each wavelength. Cameras, like eyes, have only three kinds of light sensor, each sensitive to a band of wavelengths, so the whole spectrum is squeezed into three numbers: R, G and B.
glossary.entries.colour.body.1: Squeezing loses something: many completely different spectra give the same R, G and B. This is called metamerism. Screens rely on it, using red light plus green light to make you see yellow. But change the lamp and the spectrum an object reflects changes too, so two cloths that match in daylight may stop matching.
glossary.entries.colour.body.2: RGB, HSV and Lab just give these three numbers different coordinates. Lab, for example, separates lightness from colour, which is handy when you want to change a colour without changing its lightness.
glossary.entries.colour.title: Colour, RGB and metamerism
glossary.entries.contrastive.body.0: Most photos have no labels. One way round this is to make two altered versions of an image (shifted a little, brightened or darkened, with noise added): they certainly come from the same image, and that fact can itself serve as the answer. Learning where the data supplies its own answers, without human labels, is called self-supervised learning.
glossary.entries.contrastive.body.1: Contrastive learning pulls the two views of the same image (a positive pair) together and pushes the other views in the batch (negative pairs) apart; the InfoNCE loss is written this way. SimCLR is a well-known example.
glossary.entries.contrastive.body.2: Pull together without pushing apart, and putting every image at the same point minimises the loss but tells nothing apart. This is called collapse.
glossary.entries.contrastive.title: Contrastive and self-supervised learning
glossary.entries.convlayer.body.0: A convolution layer’s window is a kernel that stops at one place after another, computing one number at each. Output side = ⌊(N + 2p − k) / s⌋ + 1, where N is the input side, k the window size, p the padding width and s the stride, how many cells it moves each time. With a stride above 1 it skips stops and the image shrinks.
glossary.entries.convlayer.body.1: The parameters depend only on the window: each filter has k × k × channels weights plus 1 bias, however big the image is. Using the same weights everywhere is called weight sharing; it saves a huge number of parameters, and lets a pattern be recognised wherever it appears.
glossary.entries.convlayer.body.2: If every output pixel were connected to every input pixel (fully connected), there would be far more parameters, and they would balloon as the image grows.
glossary.entries.convlayer.title: Convolution layers: stride, padding and parameters
glossary.entries.convolution.body.0: Give a kernel an image with a single bright dot and the output is the kernel itself: this is the impulse response. So seeing what a bright dot turns into tells you which kernel was used.
glossary.entries.convolution.body.1: But there are two ways to read a kernel. Cross-correlation lays the kernel straight over the image, multiplying matching positions and adding; convolution first rotates the kernel by 180°. A bright dot put through a convolution comes out as the kernel the right way up; through a cross-correlation, as the kernel turned by 180°.
glossary.entries.convolution.body.2: The kernel parts in this game all do cross-correlation. A symmetric kernel is unchanged by a 180° turn, so for it the two readings are the same.
glossary.entries.convolution.title: Convolution, cross-correlation and the impulse response
glossary.entries.convthm.body.0: Convolving with a kernel in space is the same as multiplying each frequency by a gain in the frequency domain, where the gain is the kernel’s spectrum. This is the convolution theorem: convolution in space is multiplication in frequency.
glossary.entries.convthm.body.1: A hard cut-off gain (keep everything below some frequency, remove everything above) turns back into a kernel with negative lobes on both sides, so rings of light and dark ripple out beside edges: this is ringing. A Gaussian-shaped gain turns back into a Gaussian, with no negative lobes and so no ringing.
glossary.entries.convthm.body.2: The wider a Gaussian, the narrower its spectrum: the more it blurs in space, the fewer frequencies it keeps.
glossary.entries.convthm.title: The convolution theorem and ringing
glossary.entries.corner.body.0: To recognise the same point in two photos, the point has to be easy to find again. On flat ground a move in any direction looks the same; on a straight edge, a move along the edge looks the same; only at a corner does a move in any direction change what you see.
glossary.entries.corner.body.1: The Harris corner detector gathers the gradients in both directions over a small patch round each pixel into a 2×2 matrix and scores it with R = det − k·trace²: when the change is large in both directions R is large and positive, a corner; a straight edge is large in only one direction, so R is negative; on flat ground R is close to 0.
glossary.entries.corner.body.2: A corner is still a corner when the image is rotated, which is why corners are often used as key points for stitching panoramas and tracking motion.
glossary.entries.corner.title: Corners and Harris
glossary.entries.depth.body.0: Converting disparity into distance uses the same reasoning as the pinhole camera: depth z = f·b / d, where f is the focal length, b the distance between the two cameras (the baseline) and d the disparity.
glossary.entries.depth.body.1: Disparity is counted in pixels, and one pixel off throws the depth off noticeably: |Δz| ≈ z²/(f·b)·|Δd|, so something twice as far has four times the error.
glossary.entries.depth.body.2: A wider baseline or a longer lens makes far things more precise, but makes the disparity of near things bigger, past the search range, and the two images look more different too. Only the product f·b matters, so you trade off “near things still match” against “far things are precise enough”.
glossary.entries.depth.title: Depth, focal length and baseline
glossary.entries.descent.body.0: Before a machine can tune its own parameters, it needs a score for “how bad is it now”. That score is the loss (the error): how far the model’s output is from the right answer, commonly the average of the squared differences.
glossary.entries.descent.body.1: Treat all the adjustable numbers as a position and the loss as a landscape, and training is walking downhill. The gradient points up the steepest slope, and each step moves “learning rate × gradient” the opposite way: this is gradient descent.
glossary.entries.descent.body.2: Too small a learning rate takes many steps; too large and you bounce from one side of the valley to the other, further each time. In a long, narrow valley the gradient keeps pointing at the walls, so the path zig-zags. A network has millions of knobs, and the principle is exactly the same.
glossary.entries.descent.title: Loss and gradient descent
glossary.entries.details.body.0: The test panel lists every test; pick one to see its details: the input, the expected output, your output, and an error map marking which cells are outside the tolerance. A failing test says why, such as how many pixels are outside the tolerance, or that the size is wrong.
glossary.entries.details.body.1: Hover over a picture to read the value in each cell and the value expected there. When the output is a single number, the expected value, the allowed range and your reading are drawn on one scale; when it is a single row, it is drawn as a curve, with an allowed band round the expected curve.
glossary.entries.details.body.2: Whichever test is selected, every part on the board shows its results for that test. On a phone, tap the test tabs along the top to switch, and find the details under “Test details” in the bottom bar.
glossary.entries.details.title: Test details
glossary.entries.detect.body.0: Sliding-window detection scores a template at every position of the picture, then thresholds and applies non-maximum suppression. Things of other sizes are found with the same detector on shrunken copies (an image pyramid), and the results are enlarged back and merged.
glossary.entries.detect.body.1: Modern detectors place a few anchors at every position and regress four corrections: the centre moves by t × the anchor's width or height, and the size is multiplied by e^t. Faster R-CNN and YOLO both work like this, and are scored with IoU and mAP.
glossary.entries.detect.title: Sliding windows, anchors and detection
glossary.entries.diffusion.body.0: A diffusion model first learns the other direction: noise is added step by step, x_t = √ᾱ·x₀ + √(1 − ᾱ)·ε, and as ᾱ falls from 1 to 0 the picture sinks into the noise. Two rounds of noise equal one with the ᾱ multiplied, so training can jump straight to any step.
glossary.entries.diffusion.body.1: The network learns to guess ε from x_t; knowing the noise, x₀ = (x_t − √(1 − ᾱ)·ε) / √ᾱ. To generate, it starts from pure noise and, step after step, guesses the noise and removes a little, until a picture never seen before appears.
glossary.entries.diffusion.title: Diffusion models
glossary.entries.disparity.body.0: The distance by which the same thing is offset between the left and right images is its disparity. Near things are offset more and far things less, so the larger the disparity, the nearer the object.
glossary.entries.disparity.body.1: When the two cameras are lined up, corresponding points are always on the same row, so the search only runs along that row: which shift of the right image matches the left one best. This is stereo matching. Random-dot images show that people can see depth without recognising any object.
glossary.entries.disparity.body.2: Each comparison uses a window round the cell. A large window resists noise but wipes out detail; a small one keeps detail but is vulnerable to noise. No window is best for every image, and methods such as multi-scale and global optimisation try to get both at once.
glossary.entries.disparity.title: Disparity and stereo matching
glossary.entries.edge.body.0: An edge is where the brightness changes suddenly over a short distance: where an object meets the background, the strokes of letters. The simplest way to measure it is the difference between neighbouring pixels: 0 on flat ground, largest at a step.
glossary.entries.edge.body.1: The neighbour difference is a discrete derivative. It has a sign: positive from dark to bright, negative from bright to dark, so the sign tells you which way the edge faces. Since the result can be negative, terrain view shows it best: an edge becomes a ridge or a trench.
glossary.entries.edge.title: Edges and derivatives
glossary.entries.epipolar.body.0: Real cameras are rarely lined up exactly, so the same point often lands on a different row. But a point in the left image fixes only a line of sight, and every possible depth along it projects into the right image onto one straight line, called the <part-ref to="epiline"></part-ref>.
glossary.entries.epipolar.body.1: The cameras’ relative position can be calibrated in advance and recorded as a 3×3 fundamental matrix F. The epipolar line of a left-image point p is l′ = F·p, written a·u′ + b·v′ + c = 0; where the point lands on that line depends on how far away it is.
glossary.entries.epipolar.body.2: So a 2-D search becomes 1-D, saving a great many comparisons. All the epipolar lines meet at one point, the epipole.
glossary.entries.epipolar.title: Epipolar lines and the fundamental matrix
glossary.entries.filter.body.0: When an output cell is computed not just from the input cell in the same place but as a weighted sum of it and its neighbours, that is filtering. If the weights are all positive and add up to 1, it is a kind of average and the image gets blurrier.
glossary.entries.filter.body.1: Averaging spreads a lone bright dot out and smooths away flickering specks. The same weights are used at every position, so wherever a pattern moves, its result moves with it.
glossary.entries.filter.title: Filtering
glossary.entries.fourier.body.0: Given a curve that is already added up, how do you tell how strong the wave at one frequency is? Multiply the signal point by point by the cos and the sin of that frequency and take the averages, giving two readings a and b. Waves at other frequencies average out to 0; only the one at that frequency remains.
glossary.entries.fourier.body.1: The amplitude is 2·√(a² + b²), however far the wave is shifted, and the phase is atan2(b, a). With cos alone, a wave shifted by 90° would measure as 0.
glossary.entries.fourier.body.2: Measuring every frequency this way is the Fourier transform. It turns an image from “how bright each position is” into “how strong the wave at each frequency is”, and transforming back loses nothing.
glossary.entries.fourier.title: The Fourier transform
glossary.entries.game.body.0: In Vision Complete, you build image-processing circuits from components. Each puzzle gives you inputs and expected outputs. Pass every test to solve it.
glossary.entries.game.body.1: You start as Probe V-0, just powered on: your sensor turns the world into a grid of numbers that you cannot read yet. Your job is to learn, step by step, to read them.
glossary.entries.game.body.2: Your progress is kept in this browser on this device: close the page and come back, and the levels you passed and the circuits you built are still there.
glossary.entries.game.title: How the game works
glossary.entries.gan.body.0: A generative adversarial network (GAN) sets two models against each other: the generator draws fake samples and the judge (the discriminator) tells real from fake. The better the judge gets, the more convincing the generator has to be.
glossary.entries.gan.body.1: Ideally the generator ends up drawing the same distribution as the real data, so the judge can only guess and its accuracy is back to 50%.
glossary.entries.gan.body.2: A common failure is mode collapse: the real data has several clusters, but the generator’s samples cover only one of them.
glossary.entries.gan.title: GANs and mode collapse
glossary.entries.gaussian.body.0: A box blur spreads a bright dot into a flat-topped square block, with hard edges and corners. A <part-ref to="gauss"></part-ref> weights the centre most and further cells less, like a bell in cross-section, so a bright dot is spread into a smooth little hill.
glossary.entries.gaussian.body.1: σ sets how wide the bell is: the larger σ, the blurrier the image. Smoothing on top of smoothing looks more and more like a Gaussian, and three box blurs in a row are almost one; that is one reason Gaussians are everywhere in vision.
glossary.entries.gaussian.title: Gaussian blur
glossary.entries.gradient.body.0: The gradient is an arrow (gx, gy): gx is how much the brightness changes for each step to the right, and gy the same going down. Think of the image as a landscape, and the arrow always points straight up the steepest slope, the way the brightness rises fastest.
glossary.entries.gradient.body.1: The arrow’s length √(gx² + gy²) says how steep it is, and its direction is atan2(gy, gx). On an edge the arrow is long and perpendicular to the edge: an edge is where the gradient is large.
glossary.entries.gradient.body.2: Work out the arrow’s length at every pixel and draw it as an image, brighter where steeper, and you have an edge strength map. It does not depend on which way an edge runs: horizontal, vertical and diagonal edges are equally bright. Set a threshold on it, and the pixels above it count as edges.
glossary.entries.gradient.title: The gradient and edge strength
glossary.entries.homogeneous.body.0: Homogeneous coordinates write the point (x, y) as three numbers (x, y, 1) and the line ax + by + c = 0 as (a, b, c). A point lies on a line exactly when their dot product is 0.
glossary.entries.homogeneous.body.1: The <part-ref to="cross"></part-ref> of two points is the line through them, and of two lines the point where they meet, (X, Y, W), standing for (X/W, Y/W); parallel lines have W = 0 and meet at infinity.
glossary.entries.homogeneous.title: Homogeneous coordinates and the cross product
glossary.entries.homography.body.0: Photograph a book at a slant and the cover is no longer a neat rectangle. The transformation that maps the points of a plane into the photo is a homography, written as a 3×3 matrix H with 8 degrees of freedom.
glossary.entries.homography.body.1: Each pair of corresponding points gives 2 equations, so at least 4 pairs are needed, and H is usually solved with DLT. An affine map has only 6 degrees of freedom and is fixed by 3 pairs, but it keeps parallel lines parallel, so it cannot fit a book seen in perspective.
glossary.entries.homography.body.2: In a real pipeline the pairs come from candidates that passed the ratio test, and RANSAC picks them by repeatedly drawing 4 pairs and counting inliers. Panorama stitching and augmented reality both work this way.
glossary.entries.homography.title: Homographies and affine maps
glossary.entries.hough.body.0: Edge detection gives a scatter of points. The Hough transform has each point vote for every line through it: a line is recorded by two numbers, its direction θ and its distance ρ from the centre, with ρ = x·cos θ + y·sin θ. A line that is really there collects many votes.
glossary.entries.hough.body.1: The votes fall into cells (bins) on the (θ, ρ) plane, a grid called the accumulator, so finding a line becomes finding a peak. With bins too fine, noise splits one line’s votes into many small peaks; too coarse, and two nearby lines merge into one peak.
glossary.entries.hough.body.2: With more parameters the number of cells grows as a power: a line has only 2 parameters, but with 8 parameters, 10 cells per dimension makes 10⁸ cells.
glossary.entries.hough.title: The Hough transform
glossary.entries.hybrid.body.0: A high-pass filter keeps only the detail: high-pass = image − low-pass, which in the frequency domain means replacing the mask H with 1 − H.
glossary.entries.hybrid.body.1: Take an image’s broad light and dark from A (its low frequencies) and its detail from B (its high frequencies), and you have a hybrid image. Up close the detail stands out and you see B; from a distance, or with narrowed eyes, the detail can no longer be made out and only A is left.
glossary.entries.hybrid.body.2: Filtering is linear: combining and then filtering gives the same result as filtering each and then combining. That lets many things that seem to need two steps be done in one.
glossary.entries.hybrid.title: High-pass and hybrid images
glossary.entries.intrinsic.body.0: In a photo, a surface’s own colour and the light falling on it are multiplied together: photo = colour × lighting. A white wall in shadow looks grey, and dark floor tiles can look bright in sunshine.
glossary.entries.intrinsic.body.1: So an edge in a photo only says “the brightness changes here”; what changed may be the colour, or just the light. A shadow on a plain wall has a hard edge too. Splitting a photo into its colour and its lighting is called intrinsic image decomposition.
glossary.entries.intrinsic.body.2: A real camera does not come with a lighting map, and brightness alone cannot pin the lighting down.
glossary.entries.intrinsic.title: Shadow or colour
glossary.entries.intro.body.0: The first time you enter a level, a few pages of “Intro” open: what the level is about, where it shows up in the real world, any new parts, and a question worth thinking about before you start. You can reopen it any time from “Intro” in the top bar.
glossary.entries.intro.body.1: Below the task there is a “Hint” button for when you are stuck. Hints are fairly direct, so it pays to try on your own first.
glossary.entries.intro.body.2: When you pass, the passed window sums up in a few lines what just happened. Most of the ideas it names have an entry in this encyclopedia.
glossary.entries.intro.title: Intros and hints
glossary.entries.invariance.body.0: Light the same scene differently and the pixel values can differ a lot, yet the right answer stays the same. When designing a feature, first ask: which changes should not change the answer? Making the answer immune to those changes is called invariance.
glossary.entries.invariance.body.1: Lighting changes come roughly in two kinds. Brightening everything (+ b on every pixel, an offset) just lifts the whole landscape and leaves the slopes as they were, so the gradient is unchanged by it. A stronger or dimmer lamp (× a on every pixel, a gain) multiplies every slope by a, so a fixed threshold stops working.
glossary.entries.invariance.title: Invariance
glossary.entries.iou.body.0: <part-ref to="iou"></part-ref> (intersection over union) = the area where two boxes overlap ÷ the area they cover together, from 0 to 1. A detected box counts as right when its IoU with the labelled box is above 0.5 (VOC).
glossary.entries.iou.body.1: Sort the detections by score: the precision at rank k = the number right in the top k ÷ k, and AP is the precisions at the right ones, added up and divided by the number labelled: the area under the precision–recall curve. The average AP over the classes is mAP.
glossary.entries.iou.title: IoU and AP
glossary.entries.kernel.body.0: Averaging and differencing are really the same operation: each output cell is a weighted sum of the small block around it. Lay the weights out in a small square and you have a kernel. Change the weights and you change the effect.
glossary.entries.kernel.body.1: Pass the kernel over the whole image, computing a weighted sum at each spot, and you have the filtered result. A kernel with just a 1 in the centre leaves the image unchanged; behind many photo-editor filters there is often just a kernel.
glossary.entries.kernel.title: Kernels
glossary.entries.kernelread.body.0: With practice, a glance at the numbers in a kernel tells you what it does. All positive and adding up to 1 means smoothing, and the more the weight is concentrated in the centre, the closer the result is to the original.
glossary.entries.kernelread.body.1: A kernel that adds up to 0 gives 0 on flat ground and responds only to change: it is a derivative. A large centre with negative surroundings is sharpening. A kernel with a single 1 is a shift: read as cross-correlation, the image moves the opposite way from where the 1 sits off-centre.
glossary.entries.kernelread.title: Reading a kernel
glossary.entries.kmeans.body.0: k-means splits data into k heaps without labels: choose k centres, give every point to its nearest centre, move each centre to the average of its heap, and repeat until nothing changes.
glossary.entries.kmeans.body.1: Splitting into two by brightness, the boundary sits halfway between the two centres. It only sees the features it is given: with brightness alone, two things of the same brightness cannot be told apart; add position as a feature and you get superpixels (SLIC).
glossary.entries.kmeans.title: k-means
glossary.entries.lambert.body.0: How much light a surface sends back is its reflectance: close to 1 for white paint, close to 0 for black. The direction a surface faces “straight out” is its normal, which you can picture as a small stick standing up from the middle of the surface.
glossary.entries.lambert.body.1: Matte surfaces roughly follow the Lambertian model: brightness = lamp strength × reflectance × cos θ, where θ is the angle between the light and the normal. Light arriving at a slant spreads the same beam over a larger area, so it is dimmer; cos 60° = 0.5, so at 60° the brightness is halved.
glossary.entries.lambert.body.2: A photo keeps only the product of the three: a dark patch may mean a weaker lamp, darker paint, or just a surface turned away. From brightness alone you cannot tell which.
glossary.entries.lambert.title: Lambertian reflection and normals
glossary.entries.layout.body.0: On a desktop the screen is a workbench: the task, hint and parts list on the left, the board in the middle and the test panel on the right. Click a part in the list to drop it in a free spot on the board; drag a wire from the dot on the right of a part to another part; select a part or wire and press Delete to remove it.
glossary.entries.layout.body.1: Drag an empty part of the board to pan, hold ⌘/Ctrl and scroll (or pinch) to zoom, and the corner buttons fit the whole circuit into view.
glossary.entries.layout.body.2: On a phone it is a tall circuit board: the inputs at the top, the outputs at the bottom and two columns of slots in between. Tap a part in the tray at the bottom to drop it into a free slot, tap two dots to wire them, and tap a wired input to unplug it; hold a block to move it to another slot, or drag it back onto the tray to remove it. Tap a block to open its panel, with its description and settings.
glossary.entries.layout.body.3: The phone’s bottom bar has “Undo”, the test details, “Clear” (tap twice) and “Run tests”. Both layouts edit the same circuit.
glossary.entries.layout.title: Desktop and phone
glossary.entries.lowpass.body.0: A filter that keeps the low frequencies and removes the high ones is called a low-pass filter. Low frequencies are broad, slow changes in brightness and high ones are fine texture, edges and noise, so a low-pass filter blurs and removes noise.
glossary.entries.lowpass.body.1: It can be done in space with a blur kernel, or in the frequency domain: transform to the spectrum, multiply by a mask centred on the middle, and transform back. The mask’s radius decides how many frequencies are kept: the smaller the radius, the blurrier the image.
glossary.entries.lowpass.title: Low-pass filtering
glossary.entries.map.body.0: On the map, each chapter follows a theme and its levels sit along a circuit trace. The chapter title is followed by the question you will explore. Level icons distinguish circuits from benches.
glossary.entries.map.body.1: A level opens once the levels before it are passed; passed levels are ticked and closed ones show a padlock. “Continue” takes you straight to the first level you have not passed yet. Turn on “Unlock all” to play any level in any order; progress is still recorded.
glossary.entries.map.body.2: Inside a level, the “Levels” button in the top bar opens a list of levels, so you can switch levels without going back to the map.
glossary.entries.map.title: The level map and chapters
glossary.entries.neuron.body.0: A neuron first computes a weighted sum w1·x1 + w2·x2 + b, then uses a sigmoid to squash the result between 0 and 1, read as “how sure”. w1·x1 + w2·x2 + b = 0 is a straight line in the plane, so one neuron is one dividing line; the larger the weights, the more decisive the judgement.
glossary.entries.neuron.body.1: But for a problem like XOR, no single straight line can separate the points, however it is placed. And with only adding, subtracting and multiplying by constants, any number of layers stays linear: two linear layers stacked are still just one straight line.
glossary.entries.neuron.body.2: Put a nonlinear activation function between the layers, and the network can draw curved boundaries. The most common is ReLU: negatives become 0 and positives pass unchanged, written max(0, x).
glossary.entries.neuron.title: Neurons and activation functions
glossary.entries.nms.body.0: Above a threshold a response map comes in patches: several cells round one corner or one dog are all strong. Non-maximum suppression keeps only the cell no smaller than everything around it: work out the largest value in the 3×3 round each cell, then check whether the cell equals it.
glossary.entries.nms.body.1: The 3×3 maximum can be taken across then down in two steps, like a separable blur. Corner detection, finding lines with Hough and object detection all end with it.
glossary.entries.nms.title: Non-maximum suppression
glossary.entries.occlusion.body.0: A classifier that answers right has not necessarily looked in the right place: in a training set where cars always stand on roads, recognising the road alone gets everything right. Such a shortcut is only found by checking where the model looks.
glossary.entries.occlusion.body.1: The occlusion experiment slides a patch over the picture cell by cell, notes how far the score drops with each place covered, and draws that as a heat map. It needs nothing from inside the model and works for a CNN or a ViT, at the price of running the model again for every position. The patch is usually grey (the dataset's average colour), and about the size of the object's parts.
glossary.entries.occlusion.body.2: Grad-CAM runs the model once: the gradient of the score with respect to the last convolutional feature maps gives each channel a weight, the maps are added with those weights, and a ReLU keeps only what supports the class. For a ViT one can look at which patches the class token attends to, but the layers and heads have to be combined (attention rollout); a single head alone is easily misleading.
glossary.entries.occlusion.title: Occlusion and heat maps
glossary.entries.overfit.body.0: The training error keeps falling, but the error on new samples falls and then rises: in the second half the model is memorising the noise in its training samples. This is overfitting. That is why part of the data is kept back for checking only: the validation set.
glossary.entries.overfit.body.1: One fix is early stopping: stop where the validation error is lowest. Another is regularisation: put a cost on large weights (L2), so the model will not bend the curve sharply just to hit a few points.
glossary.entries.overfit.body.2: If the strength λ is too small it cannot hold off overfitting; too large and the model cannot learn even the true rule, which is called underfitting. Dropout and data augmentation serve the same purpose.
glossary.entries.overfit.title: Overfitting and regularisation
glossary.entries.padding.body.0: When processing the pixels at the very edge, some neighbours fall outside the image. There is no data out there, so values have to be filled in, and what is filled in directly decides the result all round the border.
glossary.entries.padding.body.1: Padding with 0 amounts to drawing a black frame round the image: averaging on a bright background leaves a dark ring round the border, and differentiating creates a false edge there. Replicate edge treats each missing value as the nearest pixel on the edge, so no border appears out of nowhere.
glossary.entries.padding.body.2: In this game, the “Border” setting of Shift and of every filter can choose between “Pad with 0” and “Replicate edge”.
glossary.entries.padding.title: Padding mode
glossary.entries.perpixel.body.0: When each output cell is worked out only from the input cell in the same position, each on its own, it is a per-pixel operation. Multiplying by a factor brightens or darkens the whole image in proportion, adding a constant raises or lowers every cell together, and two images can be added, subtracted or multiplied cell by cell.
glossary.entries.perpixel.body.1: A per-pixel operation can change brightness, but it never knows who its neighbours are.
glossary.entries.perpixel.title: Per-pixel operations
glossary.entries.pinhole.body.0: Make a small hole in the wall of a dark box, and light from the scene can only pass through that one point, forming an upside-down image on the screen opposite. This is the pinhole camera, the earliest form of the camera.
glossary.entries.pinhole.body.1: The size of the image depends only on a ratio: x = −f·X/Z, where X is the object’s height, Z its distance from the hole and f the distance from the hole to the screen; the minus sign means the image is upside down. The further away something is, the smaller its image: this is perspective projection.
glossary.entries.pinhole.body.2: A bigger hole makes the image brighter, but light from one point spreads into a spot on the screen, so the image also gets blurrier. A lens exists to break this trade-off: open a big hole to let in more light, then bring the light back together to a point.
glossary.entries.pinhole.title: The pinhole camera and perspective projection
glossary.entries.pixel.body.0: Inside a computer, an image is a table of numbers: the picture is cut into many small squares called pixels, and each records a brightness. In this game 0 is black, 1 is white, and the values in between are shades of grey.
glossary.entries.pixel.body.1: Every method in computer vision comes down to arithmetic on these numbers.
glossary.entries.pixel.title: Pixels and images
glossary.entries.pooling.body.0: Max pooling cuts the image into 2×2 blocks and keeps only the largest value of each, halving the size. It asks only “what is the strongest value in this block”, not where in the block it is.
glossary.entries.pooling.body.1: So as long as a point moves within the same block, the result does not change, which lets a network tolerate small shifts. The price is losing the exact position inside the block.
glossary.entries.pooling.title: Max pooling
glossary.entries.posenc.body.0: Self-attention assigns weights only by how alike patches are; it does not know where each one sits. Swap two patches and the output just swaps with them: it sees a bag of patches, not a sequence.
glossary.entries.posenc.body.1: A positional encoding adds a quantity standing for position to each patch: z̃ᵢ = zᵢ + pᵢ, like a house number on every patch, so that order can enter the computation. ViT adds the positions to every patch before the first layer.
glossary.entries.posenc.title: Positional encoding
glossary.entries.ransac.body.0: When matching or finding lines, wrong points always creep in: outliers; the right ones are inliers. Fit one line to all the points and a few distant outliers can drag it off course.
glossary.entries.ransac.body.1: RANSAC takes another approach: draw at random the fewest points a model needs (2 for a line), work out the model, count how many points lie close enough to it (within δ), repeat for many rounds, and keep the one with the most support.
glossary.entries.ransac.body.2: The number of rounds comes from probability: with an inlier ratio p and n points drawn per round, reaching a success rate P needs k ≥ log(1 − P) / log(1 − pⁿ) rounds. The number of rounds is set by the inlier ratio and δ by the noise; neither can stand in for the other.
glossary.entries.ransac.title: Inliers, outliers and RANSAC
glossary.entries.ratio.body.0: Once key points are found they need pairing: take the small patch round a point in the left image and look for the most similar patch in the right one. Similarity is measured as a distance d, smaller meaning more alike; the closest is first place (distance d₁) and the next is second place (d₂).
glossary.entries.ratio.body.1: A repeating pattern (a fence of identical tiles, say) makes first and second place almost equally close; however “alike” such a match is, it cannot be trusted, and a distance threshold alone cannot stop it. The ratio test d₁ / d₂ < r accepts only matches whose first place is clearly ahead; r = 0.8 is a common choice.
glossary.entries.ratio.title: Feature matching and the ratio test
glossary.entries.receptive.body.0: The patch of input that one output pixel can “see” is its receptive field. One 3×3 layer sees 3×3, but the second layer looks at the first layer’s output, so in effect it sees 5×5; stack L layers of 3×3 and the receptive field is (2L+1)×(2L+1).
glossary.entries.receptive.body.1: Stacking small kernels to see a large area is also cheaper: three 3×3 layers have only 27 weights, while one 7×7 kernel needs 49, and nonlinearities can go in between. Networks like VGG are built this way; pooling and larger strides make the receptive field grow faster still.
glossary.entries.receptive.title: Receptive fields
glossary.entries.reparam.body.0: Draw z at random from a normal distribution and hand it to the decoder, and you can draw pictures never seen before: this is generation. Random does not mean arbitrary: the numbers mostly fall near the centre μ, more spread out the larger σ is. In a VAE (variational autoencoder), the encoder outputs this μ and σ.
glossary.entries.reparam.body.1: But the random sampling step cannot be differentiated: with a fresh draw each time, training cannot tell whether a better result came from changing μ and σ or from luck. Reparameterisation writes it as z = μ + σ·ε: all the randomness comes from the input ε, z is just a multiply and an add of μ and σ, and the gradient is perfectly clear.
glossary.entries.reparam.body.2: That is how a VAE is trained, and the part of Stable Diffusion that compresses and restores images relies on it during training too.
glossary.entries.reparam.title: VAEs and reparameterisation
glossary.entries.residual.body.0: A deeper network can express more, yet with many layers it often will not train. When layers are simply stacked, each layer’s gradient is multiplied by the weights of the other layers, and with enough factors it gets close to 0 and the loss does not budge. This is the vanishing gradient problem.
glossary.entries.residual.body.1: A residual connection adds each block’s input straight to its output: y = F(x) + x. Every block starts out “passing its input straight through” and only has to learn the difference F(x), and the gradient reaches every layer directly along the shortcut. This is how ResNet stacks networks to more than a hundred layers.
glossary.entries.residual.title: Vanishing gradients and residual connections
glossary.entries.sampling.body.0: A camera or scanner records brightness only at certain positions and lets those points stand for the continuous scene: this is sampling. With M samples you can only tell apart frequencies below M/2, a limit called the Nyquist frequency.
glossary.entries.sampling.body.1: Faster waves do not vanish: they fold back and pose as a slower wave, so frequency k looks exactly like M − k. This is aliasing, and once sampled the two can never be separated. A spinning wheel that seems to turn backwards on video, and the ripples (moiré) that float over a photo of a screen, are both aliasing.
glossary.entries.sampling.body.2: So anti-aliasing has to happen before sampling: low-pass away everything above the Nyquist frequency first, then sample. Taking photos and scanning both face the same problem.
glossary.entries.sampling.title: Sampling and aliasing
glossary.entries.score.body.0: Circuit levels are scored on two things: parts is how many parts you placed, and cost is how many arithmetic operations it takes to compute one output pixel. Lower cost is better; at equal cost, fewer parts wins.
glossary.entries.score.body.1: Your best score for each level is kept and shown on the map beside the passed level. The score does not usually affect passing, so you can come back later and improve it.
glossary.entries.score.body.2: A few levels set a limit, such as a maximum cost or a maximum number of parts. The limit is shown under the score, and until it is met, passing every test does not complete the level.
glossary.entries.score.title: Score and limits
glossary.entries.separable.body.0: Some kernels split into “a column times a row”: a 3×3 average, for example, is a 3-point horizontal average followed by a 3-point vertical one. Then filtering across once and down once gives the same result as using the whole kernel. This is separable filtering.
glossary.entries.separable.body.1: The gain is in cost: a k×k kernel takes k² multiply-adds done directly, but only 2k when split. For 3×3 that is 9 down to 6, and the bigger the kernel, the more you save. Gaussian kernels split this way too.
glossary.entries.separable.title: Separable filtering
glossary.entries.sfs.body.0: Now the other way round: from one brightness, can you work out which way a surface faces? A brightness only tells you the angle between the normal and the lamp, and a whole ring of facings has that angle, so a single photo cannot recover a unique facing.
glossary.entries.sfs.body.1: Shape from shading has to rely on extra assumptions: an even colour, a known lamp, a smooth surface. People quietly make the same assumptions when they look at a photo.
glossary.entries.sfs.body.2: Change the lamp and take another photo, and the two rings of possible facings cross at only one or two points; with three lamps you can solve for the reflectance as well. This is called photometric stereo.
glossary.entries.sfs.title: Shape from shading
glossary.entries.sharpen.body.0: The original minus a blurred copy leaves exactly what the blur wiped out: edges, fine texture and other things that change quickly. That is the detail.
glossary.entries.sharpen.body.1: Add the detail back to the original in some proportion and the contrast on either side of each edge is stretched, so the image looks sharper: this is sharpening. The USM (unsharp mask) sharpening in photo editors works this way, and comes from a darkroom trick of printing a blurred negative together with the original.
glossary.entries.sharpen.body.2: Add too much and an obvious bright and dark halo appears beside each edge. Sharpening cannot recover lost information; it only makes the changes already there stand out.
glossary.entries.sharpen.title: Sharpening and detail
glossary.entries.sobel.body.0: Real photos always carry noise: in dim light, each cell’s number comes out randomly a little too high or too low. Neighbour differences are very sensitive to this jitter, so false edges pop up even on flat ground.
glossary.entries.sobel.body.1: The fix is to smooth first and then differentiate: the noise is pushed down and the real edge stays. The Sobel operator puts both steps into one 3×3 kernel: it differentiates in one direction and smooths with weights 1, 2, 1 in the other.
glossary.entries.sobel.body.2: Sobel x measures change from left to right and Sobel y from top to bottom.
glossary.entries.sobel.title: Noise and the Sobel operator
glossary.entries.spectrum.body.0: The spectrum of a 2-D image is itself an image: each cell (kx, ky) stands for one wave, and the brighter it is, the stronger that wave is in the picture. The very centre is frequency (0, 0), the average brightness, called the DC component.
glossary.entries.spectrum.body.1: Further from the centre means faster change: the denser the stripes, the further their dots sit from the centre. Turn the stripes by 90° and the dots turn by 90° too, always lined up perpendicular to the stripes. One set of stripes shows up as a pair of dots placed symmetrically about the centre.
glossary.entries.spectrum.body.2: A blurred image keeps only a clump of low frequencies in the centre, while noise has every frequency. The game draws spectra on a log scale, so weak waves show up too.
glossary.entries.spectrum.title: Spectra and the DC component
glossary.entries.superpose.body.0: Any brightness curve can be taken apart into a set of sine waves: one amplitude for each frequency, plus a phase. That set of amplitudes is the curve’s <part-ref to="spectrum"></part-ref>.
glossary.entries.superpose.body.1: The steeper an edge, the more high frequencies it needs. A square wave uses only odd frequencies, with amplitudes falling as 1, 1/3, 1/5, 1/7; leave out the high ones and small ripples appear beside the steep edges.
glossary.entries.superpose.body.2: A blurred curve keeps only its low frequencies. Seen this way, blurring means turning the high frequencies down.
glossary.entries.superpose.title: Wave superposition
glossary.entries.tests.body.0: Each level has a few tests, and each test is an input with its expected output. Your output is compared with the expected one cell by cell: each cell may be off by a tiny amount (the tolerance), and the size must match too. Some levels let a few cells be wrong.
glossary.entries.tests.body.1: The results on the parts update all the time, but whether they pass only counts once you press “Run tests”. When every test passes, the level is complete; if not, the first failing test is selected for you. After any change to the circuit, the tests need running again.
glossary.entries.tests.body.2: Many levels also have hidden tests: they are checked on every run, but you only learn how many failed, and they are shown once you pass. If every visible test passes but a hidden one fails, your circuit may only happen to work on those particular pictures.
glossary.entries.tests.title: Tests and hidden tests
glossary.entries.training.body.0: With learnable parts, some weights in a circuit are no longer filled in by you but tuned by the machine. Whenever a circuit contains such a part, two buttons appear: “Train 1 step” and “Train 10 steps”.
glossary.entries.training.body.1: Each training step nudges every learnable weight a little in the direction that makes the error smaller. The loss curve beside the buttons shows how the error changes, on a log scale.
glossary.entries.training.body.2: Training only sees the visible tests, so the hidden tests check whether what it learned also holds for new pictures. Clearing the circuit starts the weights and the loss curve afresh.
glossary.entries.training.body.3: Some levels list a few "new samples": they take no part in training and are only checked, and the panel draws an extra error line for them. Some levels let you choose the learning rate yourself: how big each step is.
glossary.entries.training.title: Training
glossary.entries.unet.body.0: An encoder–decoder shrinks, then enlarges: shrinking looks at several cells together, so noise cancels and large structure shows; but when enlarged back, anything finer than a block is already gone.
glossary.entries.unet.body.1: A skip connection wires the encoder's full-size result straight to the decoder: the coarse path keeps out noise, the fine path keeps detail. U-Net connects every level like this, and cell and medical image segmentation depend on it.
glossary.entries.unet.title: Encoder–decoder and skip connections
glossary.entries.unlock.body.0: Passing a level often unlocks a new part, listed in the passed window. A black box you have figured out becomes your <part-ref to="shift"></part-ref>, and what you build by hand often becomes a ready-made part too, used directly from then on without your having to think about what is inside.
glossary.entries.unlock.body.1: An unlock can also be a new option in a setting.
glossary.entries.unlock.body.2: Each level’s parts list holds only the parts that level offers. The “Parts” box on the map lists every part in the game, with the ones you have earned lit up and described. When a level asks you to build something by hand, the ready-made version is put away for that level.
glossary.entries.unlock.title: The components box and unlocking
glossary.entries.upsample.body.0: Segmentation gives an answer for every pixel, so after shrinking, a network has to enlarge again. A transposed convolution zero-upsamples to twice the size, then fills the gaps with a kernel, which decides which neighbours fill each gap and in what proportion, and can be learnt.
glossary.entries.upsample.body.1: Max unpooling puts each maximum kept by pooling back in the cell it came from, with the rest 0, so details are not smeared over a whole block.
glossary.entries.upsample.title: Transposed convolution and unpooling
glossary.entries.views.body.0: Everything in a circuit is a grid of numbers, but you can draw it in different ways. A single number is drawn as a reading and a single row as a waveform; a 2-D image starts out drawn as pixels, and later levels bring in four more ways: profile, terrain, spectrum and slope.
glossary.entries.views.body.1: “Pixels” draws brightness as grey; an image with negative values puts 0 at mid-grey. “Terrain” treats brightness as height: blurring rounds off the hills and edges are cliffs. “Slope” draws contour lines and arrows pointing where the image brightens fastest. “Profile” draws the brightness along one row as a curve; drag on the picture to change row. <part-ref to="spectrum"></part-ref> shows how strong the wave at each frequency is, with frequency (0, 0) at the centre.
glossary.entries.views.body.2: Each part can switch its own view; on a desktop, “Draw all as” at the bottom left of the board switches every image part at once, and the button beside it restores the level’s default views. Changing the view does not change the circuit and needs no new test run.
glossary.entries.views.title: Ways of drawing
glossary.entries.wave.body.0: A wave is a stripe pattern whose brightness rises and falls regularly. A wave along a row takes just four numbers: the average brightness c, the amplitude A (how far light and dark differ), the frequency k (how many cycles across the whole width) and the phase φ (how far the whole wave is slid along).
glossary.entries.wave.body.1: A wave in an image also has a direction: kx cycles across and ky cycles down. The stripes always run perpendicular to the arrow (kx, ky), and the longer the arrow, the denser the stripes.
glossary.entries.wave.body.2: The smoothest waves are sinusoids (cos or sin). Any pattern, however complex, is many such waves added together.
glossary.entries.wave.title: Waves: amplitude, frequency, phase and direction
glossary.entries.wiremode.body.0: On the phone’s circuit board, wires soon tangle once there are a few parts. The wire switch at the top right of the board cycles through three displays: “All wires”, “No input wires” (the wires leaving the input parts are not drawn) and “No wires”.
glossary.entries.wiremode.body.1: Hiding wires does not change the circuit. Each wired input has a small tag beside it naming the part it reads from, and while a dot is picked, the wires of its own part are still drawn.
glossary.entries.wiremode.body.2: The choice is remembered in this browser and stays the same from level to level.
glossary.entries.wiremode.title: Wire display

level.0-1.intro.0.t: Inside a computer, a photo is not a picture but a table of numbers: the image is cut into many small squares called pixels, and each one records a brightness. In this game 0 is black, 1 is white, and in between are shades of grey.
level.0-1.intro.1.t: Computer vision works out useful information from this table of numbers: where the edges are, whether there is a person in the picture, how far away things are. Every method in this course comes down to arithmetic on these numbers.

level.0-1.intro.2.t: This level gets you used to the workbench: "Input" is the image from the camera, "Output" is the image you hand in, and the parts you wire up in between form a circuit. Each test compares your output with the expected one, cell by cell.

level.0-10.intro.0.t: On a factory line, a camera photographs every part and compares it with a photo of a good one, picking out the faulty ones. The last three levels of this chapter take place at such an inspection station.
level.0-10.intro.1.t: Two inputs: the "Reference" is a photo of a good part, and the "Part" is the one on the belt, already lined up. The part itself has light and dark areas.
level.0-10.intro.2.fig.caption: Set 1: reference, part and the expected mask
level.0-10.intro.2.t: Your task in this level: dents on the part are darker than on the reference. Output 1 on the dents and 0 everywhere else.

level.0-11.after: Light multiplies: brightness = lamp × surface. Multiplying back by 1 ÷ 0.8 = 1.25 restores the lighting the reference was taken under, and only then is the comparison fair. Adjusting the threshold alone fails: bright areas lose more to the dim lamp than dark areas lose to a dent.
level.0-11.intro.0.t: The station's lamp grows dimmer with use. Parts photographed now get only 80% of the light the reference was photographed under.
level.0-11.intro.1.t: With the lamp dimmer, the part is darker than the reference everywhere, yet nothing is wrong with it. The station must not raise alarms all over because of that.

level.0-11.intro.2.t: Your task in this level: again, mark only the dents. Something to think about: with the lamp 20% dimmer, how much darker does a bright area get, and how much a dark one?
level.0-11.tasks.0-11.brief: The station's lamp has aged to 80% of its old brightness: the part photographed now is darker all over, while the reference was taken before. Mark only the dents; the dimmer lamp must not set off alarms everywhere.

level.0-12.after: The station does three things: restore the lighting, subtract the reference cell by cell, then threshold each side and combine. Machine-vision inspection in factories often starts out exactly like this: a reference, alignment, a comparison.
level.0-12.intro.0.t: The inspection station is about to go live. Besides dents, parts may have scratches, which catch the light and look brighter than the reference.

level.0-4.after: Each pixel is worked out on its own, leaving the others alone. This is a per-pixel operation: it changes brightness, but never knows who its neighbours are.
level.0-4.intro.0.t: On a film camera's negative, light and dark are reversed: the sky looks black and a white shirt looks dark. Printing reverses them again to bring the picture back to normal. Doctors reading X-rays also often switch between positive and negative.
level.0-4.intro.1.t: In a digital image, inverting means replacing the number in every cell: 0 becomes 1, 1 becomes 0, 0.3 becomes 0.7. The photo is still the same photo, just with light and dark swapped.
level.0-4.intro.2.t: Why "1 minus the input"? Brightness always lies between 0 and 1. Multiply each cell by −1 alone and a dark 0.3 becomes −0.3 while a bright 0.9 becomes −0.9: light and dark are swapped, but every number has dropped below 0, darker than black. Add 1 to every cell and the whole picture is lifted back into 0 … 1: −0.3 + 1 = 0.7 and −0.9 + 1 = 0.1. So "multiply by −1, then add 1" is 1 − input: what was brighter is now darker.
level.0-4.intro.3.t: The parts in this level are all simple: <part-ref to="part:const"></part-ref> always outputs the same number; <part-ref to="part:mul"></part-ref> and <part-ref to="part:add"></part-ref> multiply and add two things cell by cell. When a number meets a picture, the number applies to every cell.

level.0-7.intro.0.t: Shop security cameras, traffic counters at junctions and free-space signs in car parks often have to answer the same question: what is new in the picture? The camera does not move and the background barely changes; the only thing that changes is whatever comes in.
level.0-7.intro.1.t: This level has two inputs: "Scene" is taken now, and "Empty scene" is a reference taken when nobody was there. The output is an image of only 0s and 1s, called a mask: 1 marks the cells the intruder covers, and everything else is 0.
level.0-7.intro.2.t: This is the first level with two input pictures. The new parts <part-ref to="part:sub"></part-ref> and <part-ref to="part:add"></part-ref> subtract and add two pictures cell by cell: each cell of a − b is that cell of a minus that cell of b.

level.0-8.after: Image height depends only on a ratio: x = −f·X/Z. The farther the screen is from the hole and the nearer the object, the bigger the image, and it is always upside down. The bigger the hole, the bigger the spot D·(Z+f)/Z that light from one point spreads into on the screen, so the image gets brighter and blurrier; moving the screen closer also makes it brighter.
level.0-8.intro.0.t: More than two thousand years ago, the Mohist Canon recorded that if you open a small hole in the wall of a dark room, the scene outside forms an upside-down image on the opposite wall. This is the pinhole camera; the dark room with the hole is called a camera obscura, the earliest form of the camera.
level.0-8.intro.1.t: On the bench, from left to right, are an arrow, a board with a hole in it and a screen. Z is the distance from the arrow to the board, f is the distance from the board to the screen, and the hole's diameter is D, with a few sizes to choose from. A small extra picture shows the image on the screen as seen from the front.
level.0-8.intro.2.t: Two things to think about: what decides how big the image on the screen is? And what happens to the image when the hole is made bigger or smaller?
level.0-8.intro.3.t: Your task in this level: make the image on the screen meet the requirements listed beside the bench. The bench shows live whether each one is met.

level.1-1.after: The output no longer looks only at its own pixel, but at a weighted sum of its neighbours. This is filtering.
level.1-1.intro.0.t: So far, each output cell has looked only at the cell in the same position in the input. This chapter changes that: when computing a cell, also look at the neighbours around it.
level.1-1.intro.1.t: The simplest example is averaging. Replace a cell with the average of itself and its neighbours, and a lone bright dot gets spread out while flickering specks get smoothed away. A phone's night mode uses the same kind of trick to suppress noise.
level.1-1.intro.2.t: From this chapter on, add, subtract and multiply are one part, <part-ref to="part:arith"></part-ref>: choose +, −, × or ÷ on the part. ÷ is new: a ÷ b divides each cell of a by the same cell of b. There is also a new part, the <part-ref to="part:merge"></part-ref>: it has three inputs and adds the pictures wired into them cell by cell; an empty input is skipped.
level.1-1.intro.3.t: A new way of drawing, "Profile": the brightness along one row of the picture as a curve; drag on the picture to change row. Switch to it with the drawing buttons on a part or in the test area.

level.1-10.after: You can now work back from a result to its kernel. All positive and summing to 1 is smoothing, and the more concentrated, the closer to the original. A kernel that sums to 0 responds only to change: a derivative. A large centre with negative neighbours is sharpening. A single 1 is a shift, moving the opposite way from where the 1 sits.
level.1-10.intro.0.fig.caption: A kernel passing over the whole image
level.1-10.intro.0.t: This chapter's average, Gaussian, difference and sharpen, along with the shift that moves an image by one pixel, can all be written as a 3×3 kernel. With practice, one look at an image before and after should tell you which kernel was used.
level.1-10.intro.1.t: Each round, the bench shows an input and an output. Each of the four parts below is a kernel, with its numbers laid out the way the <part-ref to="kernel3"></part-ref> part reads them. Pick the one that made this output.
level.1-10.intro.2.t: There are ten rounds, and eight right answers pass. Later rounds give you less time, and you can switch the timer off to practise first. Something to think about: without working it out cell by cell, just glancing at the numbers in a kernel, how do you recognise it?
Each round shows an input, an output and four 3×3 kernels. Pick the kernel that produced the output.
level.1-10.tasks.1-10.brief: Look at the input and the output, and pick the 3×3 kernel that made it (read the way the <part-ref to="kernel3"></part-ref> part reads it). Get 8 of 10 rounds right to pass; it gets faster as you go.
level.1-10.tasks.1-10.hint: All weights positive, summing to 1: softer. Positives and negatives cancelling, summing to 0: flat areas become 0. A single 1: the whole image shifts by one pixel.

level.1-11.after: Padding with 0 draws a black frame round the image, and averaging mixes that black in. Built from shifts that replicate the edge, the average does not darken.
level.1-11.intro.0.fig.caption: Zero-padded shift: the leftmost column turns black
level.1-11.intro.0.t: When you shift by one pixel, the numbers for the outermost column have to come from outside the image. There is no data out there, so the Shift part has always padded with 0, which is black. But what a camera captures does not suddenly turn black at the image border: that column is fake.
level.1-11.intro.1.t: A more natural way to pad is to copy: treat each missing cell outside the image as equal to the nearest pixel on the edge. This is called replicate edge. Photo editors handle the image border this way when they enlarge or blur a photo.
level.1-11.intro.2.fig.caption: A plain 3×3 average of an image on a bright background
level.1-11.intro.2.t: On a dark background you cannot see the problem; switch to a bright one and it shows. Blur a photo of the sky and a dark ring appears round the edges, like a frame that was never there.

level.1-11.intro.3.t: This level has two tasks, and neither has a ready-made setting to pick: you build both yourself. First, from Shift and Arithmetic, build a shift right by one pixel whose leftmost column is copied from the original; once built, it becomes an option in the Shift part's "Border" setting.

level.1-15.after: A larger Gaussian blur turns the grain and the thin strokes into a faint grey with almost no slope, while a paper edge, where large areas of light and dark meet, is still a slope after blurring. To look for things of a certain size, blur to that size first: this idea of "scale" will keep coming back. A scanning app finding the four sides of a page starts with exactly this pipeline: blur away the noise and the text, take gradients without inventing edges at the border, then threshold. The edges found are later fitted with four straight lines, so a page photographed at an angle can be straightened.

level.1-15.intro.1.t: The text on the paper has edges too, lots of them: every stroke is a dark line with an edge on each side. But the scanner only wants the paper's four sides.

level.1-3.after: Horizontal first, then vertical: nine multiply-adds become six. You can save like this whenever a kernel splits into a row times a column. This is separable filtering; the bigger the kernel, the more you save.
level.1-3.intro.0.t: <level-ref to="1-1"></level-ref> and <level-ref to="1-2"></level-ref> looked only left and right, or up and down; this one looks all the way round: each cell becomes the average of the nine cells in the 3×3 block around it. Horizontal and vertical are treated alike, and this is called a box blur.
level.1-3.intro.1.t: This level adds a limit: the cost, which counts how many multiplications and additions it takes to compute one output cell. A phone photo has over ten million pixels and video runs at dozens of frames a second, so saving one operation per cell adds up to a lot.
level.1-3.intro.2.fig.caption: A bright dot: the expected output spreads it into a small 3×3 block
level.1-3.intro.2.t: Your task in this level: make a 3×3 average with a cost of no more than 6. The most direct circuit goes over the limit, so you need to find a cheaper method.
level.1-3.tasks.1-3.brief: Replace each pixel with the average of the nine cells in the 3×3 block around it. The cost must not exceed 6.

level.1-4.after: Follow the bright-dot test through all three averaging parts. The first spreads the dot into a flat-topped square. The next two spread the response further and give more weight to the centre than to the edges. Repeated neighbourhood averaging approximates Gaussian smoothing. A wider smoothing response attenuates wider details too.
level.1-4.intro.0.fig.caption: A 3×3 average applied to a bright dot, in terrain view
level.1-4.intro.0.t: Box blur has a flaw: it spreads a bright dot into a flat-topped square block, with hard edges and corners. But a point of light shot through an out-of-focus lens is round, fading gradually outwards from the centre.
level.1-4.intro.1.t: This soft blur is called a <part-ref to="gauss"></part-ref>: the weight is largest at the centre and smaller further out, and a slice through it looks like a bell. The larger σ, the wider the bell and the blurrier the image. It is the blur photo editors use most.
level.1-4.intro.2.t: A new way of drawing, "Terrain": brightness becomes height, so bright places are hills and dark places are valleys.
level.1-4.intro.3.fig.caption: Set 1: bright dot
level.1-4.intro.3.t: Your task in this level: you have no Gaussian, only the 3×3 average, yet you must produce almost exactly the target result. In terrain view, the expected output for a bright dot is a smooth little hill.
level.1-4.tasks.1-4.brief: Make the same soft blur as the target (a Gaussian with σ ≈ 1.4). All you have is the 3×3 average.

level.1-5.after: The original minus the blurred image leaves exactly the detail (the high frequencies). Add the detail back and the image becomes "sharper".
level.1-5.intro.0.t: Darkroom photographers had an odd trick: print the original negative stacked with a deliberately blurred copy, and the photo comes out clearer. The "USM sharpening" (unsharp mask) in photo editors comes from this technique.
level.1-5.intro.1.fig.caption: Gaussian blur, σ = 1
level.1-5.intro.1.t: <part-ref to="gauss"></part-ref> is the part you earned in <level-ref to="1-4"></level-ref>. σ controls how wide the blur is.
level.1-5.intro.2.t: Something to think about: what is left in the difference image "original − blurred"? Why does adding it back to the original make the image look sharper?
level.1-5.intro.3.fig.caption: Set 1: square, in terrain view
level.1-5.intro.3.t: Your task in this level: build the sharpening from the formula. In terrain view, the expected output has an extra ridge and an extra dip beside every step.
level.1-5.tasks.1-5.brief: Make the details clearer: output = original + 1.5 × (original − blurred). Blur with a Gaussian of σ = 1.

level.1-6.after: This is the signed forward difference along x. Flat areas give zero, dark-to-bright steps give a positive response, and bright-to-dark steps give a negative one. A ramp also responds: equal increases between pixels give a constant difference away from the image boundary. These differences measure local intensity change and help locate edges. To measure changes along y, subtract the current pixel from the pixel below.
level.1-6.intro.0.t: When you look at a picture, the first thing you notice is outlines: where an object meets the background, the folds in clothing, the strokes of letters. In a digital image, what these places have in common is that the brightness changes suddenly over a very short distance. That is an edge.
level.1-6.intro.1.t: Finding edges is the most basic step in vision. Scanning apps use it to find the four sides of a sheet of paper, and lane-keeping systems use it to find lane markings.
level.1-6.intro.2.fig.caption: Set 1: a step, in terrain view
level.1-6.intro.2.t: Your task in this level: for every cell, output "right neighbour − self". The result can be negative, which is hard to read in greyscale; terrain view shows the rises and falls more clearly.
level.1-6.tasks.1-6.brief: Wire up “right pixel − current pixel,” then compare the first two steps. What happens to the edge response when light and dark swap?

level.1-7.after: You used a 3×3 average to reduce noise, a horizontal difference to measure intensity change, and a threshold to keep strong responses. The Sobel filters you unlock also combine differentiation and smoothing. Sobel x takes a horizontal difference with weighted vertical smoothing, while Sobel y swaps the two directions.
level.1-7.intro.0.t: Real photos always carry noise: in dim light the sensor receives little light, and each cell's number comes out randomly a little too high or too low. Zoom into a photo taken at night and the grain you see is noise.
level.1-7.intro.1.t: The edge detection from <level-ref to="1-6"></level-ref> was accurate on clean images. In this level every cell jitters slightly, and the areas on either side of the step that should be flat are full of small bumps.
level.1-7.intro.2.t: Something to think about: how does a real step differ from the jitter caused by noise?
level.1-7.intro.3.fig.caption: Set 1: a noisy step
level.1-7.intro.3.t: Your task in this level: output 1 only at the real step and 0 everywhere else. Each test has its step in a different place, always dark on the left and bright on the right.
level.1-7.tasks.1-7.brief: The photo is noisy. Output 1 only at the real step (every step is dark on the left, bright on the right).

level.1-8.after: Whatever a bright dot is turned into is the "stamp" of the processing: every input pixel presses one, moved to its place, multiplied by its weight and added up. Arrange the weights in a small 3×3 grid and you have a kernel.
level.1-8.intro.0.t: The three-point average, the box blur and the differences all add up a few shifted copies of the picture, each multiplied by a number. A different set of shifts and numbers gives a different effect.
level.1-8.intro.1.fig.caption: Set 1: one bright dot goes in
level.1-8.intro.1.t: Someone processed a few pictures with such a set of shifts and numbers, and you can only see the inputs and outputs. The first test is a single bright dot.
level.1-8.intro.2.t: Your task in this level: build the same processing out of shifts, constants, multiplications and additions. Something to think about: what does a single bright dot turn into?
level.1-8.tasks.1-8.brief: Someone processed these images with a weighted sum of neighbours. Build the same processing out of shifts, constants, multiplications and additions.

level.1-9.after: A single bright pixel is a discrete impulse. Its output is the filter’s impulse response and lets you recover the weights. Convolution places the kernel around the impulse in its original orientation. This part performs cross-correlation, so its output is the kernel rotated 180° around the impulse. The dot reveals the orientation, and the square and letter test the same weights.
level.1-9.intro.0.fig.caption: The default kernel: output unchanged
level.1-9.intro.0.t: The <part-ref to="kernel3"></part-ref> you earned in <level-ref to="1-8"></level-ref>: you fill in the nine weights. By default only the centre is 1, so the output is identical to the input.
level.1-9.intro.1.t: Behind photo-editor filters and in-camera sharpening there is often just a kernel. This level turns that around: someone has processed a few images with a kernel, and from only the inputs and outputs you must find that kernel.
level.1-9.intro.2.fig.caption: Set 3: letter F
level.1-9.intro.2.t: Your task in this level: dial your kernel in until it matches, so that all three tests pass.

level.10-1.after: IoU lies between 0 and 1: 1 is a perfect overlap, 0 is not touching at all. A detector's box only counts as right when its IoU with the labelled box is large enough.
level.10-1.intro.0.t: An object detector describes each candidate with a class, a confidence score and a bounding box. The class tells you what it is, the score ranks candidates, and the box coordinates give location and size. This level holds the class fixed and compares the predicted box with a labelled box.
level.10-1.intro.1.fig.caption: Set 1: slightly off
level.10-1.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: two boxes drawn as masks; output their intersection over union, with the formula in the brief.
level.10-1.tasks.10-1.brief: Two boxes drawn as masks (1 inside the box). Output their intersection over union, IoU = area of the intersection ÷ area of the union.
level.10-1.tasks.10-1.hidden.0.label: Identical
level.10-1.tasks.10-1.hidden.1.label: Not overlapping
level.10-1.tasks.10-1.hint: The intersection is the two masks multiplied cell by cell. The union = the two areas added, minus the part counted twice. Areas measured with <part-ref to="mean"></part-ref> are all off by the same factor.

level.10-10.after: The same detector finds small things on the original and large things on a shrunken copy, and the results are enlarged back and merged: this is multi-scale detection on an image pyramid. FPN does the same thing inside the network.
level.10-10.intro.0.t: Some boxes on the shelf are small and some large, and the large boxes have marks twice the size.
level.10-10.intro.1.fig.caption: One big, one small
level.10-10.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: mark a small X with a point and a large X with a 2×2 block.
level.10-10.tasks.10-10.brief: The shelf has small boxes and boxes twice the size, with marks twice as big. Output 1 at the centre of a small X, and a 2×2 block at the centre of a large X.
level.10-10.tasks.10-10.hidden.0.label: Only large

level.10-11.after: Template scores, several scales, non-maximum suppression, each X marked exactly once: the simplest detector. Replace the template with learnt convolutions and add box regression, and you have a real object-detection network, its results measured with the IoU and AP you built.
level.10-11.intro.0.t: A real photo is grainy and a little blurred, with large and small boxes mixed.
level.10-11.intro.1.fig.caption: One big, one small
level.10-11.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: mark each X exactly once.
level.10-11.tasks.10-11.brief: A grainy, slightly blurred photo of a shelf, with large and small boxes. Mark each X once: a point for a small X, a 2×2 block for a large one.

level.10-2.after: The corrections are scaled by the anchor's size, so big and small boxes use the same numbers; width and height go through e to the power, so whatever the sign of a correction, the box never gets a negative width. Faster R-CNN and YOLO both regress boxes like this.
level.10-2.intro.0.t: A detector does not draw boxes out of nothing: it first places a few anchors of fixed size at every position, then estimates how far to move them and how much to stretch them.
level.10-2.intro.1.fig.caption: Nudged right
level.10-2.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: by the formula in the brief, work out the box from the anchor and the four corrections.
level.10-2.tasks.10-2.brief: The detector places an anchor box first, then gives four corrections. The box centre = the anchor centre + correction × the anchor's width (or height); the box width = the anchor width × e^tw, and the height likewise.
level.10-2.tasks.10-2.hidden.0.label: Made smaller
level.10-2.tasks.10-2.hint: Each output is a short formula of its own.
