level.10-3.after: The same corrections move a small anchor a little and a large one a lot: the corrections are relative. A detector places anchors of several sizes and aspect ratios at every position, regressing and scoring them all together.
level.10-3.intro.0.t: Several anchors of different sizes often sit at the same position.
level.10-3.intro.1.fig.caption: Nudged right
level.10-3.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: apply the same corrections to a row of anchors and output a row of boxes.
level.10-3.tasks.10-3.brief: Three anchors, small, medium and large, sit at the same place in a row. The same corrections apply to each; output the three boxes.

level.10-4.after: Slide a template over the picture scoring every position, then apply a threshold: this is sliding-window detection. A convolutional network does the same thing, except that the templates are learnt and stacked layer on layer.
level.10-4.intro.0.t: The most direct way to detect: move a template over the picture cell by cell, scoring at each place how alike it looks.
level.10-4.intro.1.fig.caption: First set
level.10-4.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: the boxes on the shelf carry X or O marks; output 1 only at the centre of each X.

level.10-5.after: When several positions round one object pass the threshold, you get several overlapping boxes. Non-maximum suppression keeps only the strongest round about: it is almost always a detector's last step.
level.10-5.intro.0.t: A detector proposes boxes at many locations. Several candidates can report the same object. Keep the high-scoring candidate first, then decide which overlapping lower-scoring candidates should survive.
level.10-5.intro.1.t: A dog covers several pixels, and several nearby positions all look like a dog. A detector often draws several boxes for one dog.

level.10-6.intro.0.t: The <part-ref to="iou"></part-ref> in the tray outputs the intersection over union of two box masks: the overlap divided by the area they cover together.

level.10-6.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: if the IoU is large enough the detection counts as right; output 1.

level.10-7.after: The running total covers 16 cells with only 4 rounds of "shift and add", the shift doubling each time. AP is the area under the precision–recall curve: the earlier the right ones, the higher the score, and missed labels raise the denominator.
level.10-7.intro.0.t: A detector gives a list of boxes, each with a score. Sort them by score, check each in turn for right or wrong, and the detector can be given an overall mark.
level.10-7.intro.1.t: The inputs of this level are the sorted rights and wrongs (a row of sixteen 0s and 1s), the ranks 1 to 16, and how many were labelled in all.
level.10-7.intro.2.fig.caption: Right and wrong in turn
level.10-7.intro.2.t: Your task in this level: work out AP by the formula in the brief.
level.10-7.tasks.10-7.brief: The detections are sorted by score, high to low, each marked right (1) or wrong (0). The precision at rank k = the number right in the top k ÷ k. AP = the precisions at each right rank, added up, ÷ G.
level.10-7.tasks.10-7.hidden.0.label: Right only at the end
level.10-7.tasks.10-7.hint: "The number right in the top k" is a running total: every cell plus all the cells to its left. Shift now has a "Steps" setting: add the one 1 cell to the left, then the one 2 cells to the left…

level.10-7.tasks.10-7.tests.1.label: Right and wrong in turn
level.10-7.tasks.10-7.tests.2.label: A few missed
level.10-7.title: The ranking
level.10-8.after: mAP is the average of the per-class APs: a rare class counts as much as a common one, so a detector cannot just do well on the common classes. Almost every detection result reported in papers is this number.
level.10-8.intro.0.t: The <part-ref to="apMeter"></part-ref> in the tray reads right or wrong in score order, the ranks and the number labelled G, and outputs the AP.
level.10-8.intro.1.fig.caption: One good, one poor
level.10-8.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: each of two classes has its own ranking; output the average of their APs.
level.10-8.tasks.10-8.brief: The detector recognises two kinds of thing, each with its own ranking. Output the average of the two classes' APs (mAP).

level.2-1.after: c sets the middle line, the average brightness; A sets the height of the swing, the contrast; k sets how many cycles fit in the row, the density of the stripes; and φ sets which way the stripes are shifted. As a formula: c + A·cos(2π·k·x/32 + φ).
level.2-1.intro.0.t: So far we have looked at neighbours: how much a pixel differs from the ones beside it. This chapter takes another view and sees a picture as many waves added together. It starts with the simplest thing: one wave.
level.2-1.intro.1.t: A wave is stripes of light and dark that rise and fall regularly, like a zebra crossing or light through a blind. The number of times "dark—light—dark" appears along a row is the number of cycles; the more cycles, the denser the stripes and the higher the frequency.
level.2-1.intro.2.t: Your task in this level: turn the knobs on the bench until your wave lies on the target. Each step opens one knob. Something to think about: what does each knob change about the wave?

level.2-1.tasks.2-1.bench.knobs.c.label: Average c
level.2-1.tasks.2-1.bench.knobs.k.label: Frequency k
level.2-1.tasks.2-1.bench.stages.0.note: Only c turns in this step. Lay your wave (solid) on the target (dashed), and watch how the two rows of pixels below change.
level.2-1.tasks.2-1.bench.stages.0.title: Average c
level.2-1.tasks.2-1.bench.stages.0.win: c moves the whole wave up or down: the row gets lighter or darker all at once, and the contrast stays the same.
level.2-1.tasks.2-1.bench.stages.1.note: Only A turns in this step.
level.2-1.tasks.2-1.bench.stages.1.title: Amplitude A
level.2-1.tasks.2-1.bench.stages.1.win: A is the height of the swing: the bigger A, the lighter the light parts and the darker the dark ones, and the clearer the stripes. At A = 0 only a flat grey is left.
level.2-1.tasks.2-1.bench.stages.2.note: Only k turns in this step.
level.2-1.tasks.2-1.bench.stages.2.title: Frequency k
level.2-1.tasks.2-1.bench.stages.2.win: k is how many whole cycles the row goes through: k = 5 makes five bright stripes. The bigger k, the denser the stripes.
level.2-1.tasks.2-1.bench.stages.3.note: Only φ turns in this step.
level.2-1.tasks.2-1.bench.stages.3.title: Phase φ
level.2-1.tasks.2-1.bench.stages.3.win: φ slides the whole wave sideways: the stripes move, while their density and contrast stay the same. A shift of 2π brings it back to where it was.
level.2-1.tasks.2-1.bench.stages.4.note: All four knobs are open. First see where the two lines differ, then turn the knob that matches.
level.2-1.tasks.2-1.bench.stages.4.title: All four
level.2-1.tasks.2-1.bench.stages.4.win: Four numbers settle a wave exactly: c + A·cos(2π·k·x/32 + φ).
level.2-1.tasks.2-1.brief: A wave is set by four numbers: c, A, k and φ. Each step opens one knob: lay your wave on the target. In the last step all four are open.

level.2-10.after: High-pass = image − low-pass, that is, the mask 1 − H. A keeps only its broad outline and B only its edges and fine texture. Added together, the detail wins up close; from afar, or with squinted eyes, the detail disappears and only A is left. Filtering is linear, so low-pass(A − B) + B gives the same result with a single transform.
level.2-10.intro.0.t: There is a famous kind of picture: up close it shows one person, but step back a few metres and it becomes someone else. It is called a hybrid image, created by researchers in 2006, and it relies on exactly the frequencies this chapter is about.
level.2-10.intro.1.t: From far away, or when you squint, fine lines can't be made out and your eyes only see large areas of light and dark; up close, the detail stands out most. If an image takes its large light and dark areas from one picture and its detail from another, it looks different near and far.
level.2-10.intro.2.t: This level has two inputs, A and B. The output should be A's broad outline (low frequencies) plus B's detail (high frequencies). You already know how to get A's half; how to get B's half is the puzzle here.

level.2-11.after: With M samples you can only tell apart frequencies below M/2 (the Nyquist frequency). Faster waves do not vanish: they fold back and pose as a slower wave (k poses as M − k). This is aliasing, and once sampled the two can no longer be separated. So frequencies above M/2 must be removed before sampling: low-pass first, then sample.
level.2-11.intro.0.t: A camera taking a photo and a scanner scanning a page both turn a continuously varying scene into a grid of numbers. This is called sampling: recording values at only some positions and letting them stand for the whole curve.
level.2-11.intro.1.t: Sampling can do strange things. A fast-spinning wheel in a video sometimes seems to turn backwards; photograph a computer screen with your phone and rippling patterns appear that were never there. Where do these patterns come from?
level.2-11.intro.2.t: The bench draws a real wave, the samples taken from it, and what it looks like if you only see those samples. Three small experiments each ask one thing: can one wave pose as another? How few samples can you get away with and still recognise it? What can you do before sampling?
level.2-11.intro.3.t: In this level: complete the three experiments, each with just one thing to adjust. Each time, compare what the samples suggest with the real wave, and see where they differ.

level.2-2.after: A square wave uses only odd frequencies, with amplitudes falling as 1, 1/3, 1/5, 1/7. The steeper an edge, the more high frequencies it needs; stop at frequency 7 and a ripple always remains beside the steep edge. Any curve can be split into waves like this: that is the Fourier series. Each sine wave cancels itself out and averages 0, so however they are stacked, the row averages to the middle line.
level.2-2.intro.0.t: <level-ref to="2-1"></level-ref>'s stripes were a single clean wave. But real pictures have squares, letters and edges, and none of them looks like a wave. What shapes can you make by adding waves of different frequencies together?
level.2-2.intro.1.t: Sound works the same way: a piano and a violin playing the same note sound different, because the waves of different pitch mixed in them come in different proportions.

level.2-3.after: Multiply a probe wave with the curve point by point and average: the other frequencies cancel, leaving half the amplitude of the wave at the probe's frequency, and twice that is its amplitude. Change the probe's frequency to measure another wave.
level.2-3.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="2-2"></level-ref> you stacked the waves yourself, so you knew how strong each one was. The other way round: given a curve already stacked, how do you find how much k = 3 wave is in it? A tuner recognising which note you play does this kind of thing.
level.2-3.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: turn the probe's frequency on the bench, first to find the one whose product does not average to 0, then to read one wave's amplitude out of a mixed curve. Something to think about: when does the product lean to one side overall?

level.2-3.tasks.2-3.bench.stages.0.win: Only when the probe has the input's frequency does the product lean to one side, so its average is not 0; when they differ, plus and minus cancel and the average is 0.
level.2-3.tasks.2-3.bench.stages.1.note: The input is several waves mixed together; the one at frequency 5 has amplitude 0.30. Read it with the probe: the reading is the product's average times a number.

level.2-3.tasks.2-3.bench.stages.1.win: The other frequencies all cancel in the average, leaving half the amplitude of the frequency-5 wave: a cos times itself averages ½, so the reading takes a factor of 2.
level.2-3.tasks.2-3.brief: The input is a curve and the probe is a wave whose frequency you choose. The two are multiplied point by point, and the bench draws the product and its average. First find the probe whose average is not 0, then read one wave's amplitude out of a mixed curve.

level.2-4.after: One frequency takes two probes: cos measures the part lined up with it, sin the part a quarter of a cycle off, and √(a² + b²) puts them together into the amplitude, however far the wave is shifted.
level.2-4.intro.0.t: <level-ref to="2-3"></level-ref>'s inputs all lined up neatly with the probe. In a real curve, though, a wave need not start at its brightest: it may be shifted sideways.
level.2-4.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: shift the input and see whether the probe still measures it, then find a way of reading that is right however far the wave is shifted.

level.2-4.tasks.2-4.bench.stages.0.note: The input is a wave of frequency 3 and amplitude 0.30, and the probe is frequency 3 too. Turn how far the input is shifted, watch how the probe's reading (average × 2) changes, and make it read 0.
level.2-4.tasks.2-4.bench.stages.0.statu: The probe still measures part of it.
level.2-4.tasks.2-4.bench.stages.0.title: The wave it cannot see
level.2-4.tasks.2-4.bench.stages.0.win: Shifted by a quarter of a cycle, the cos probe reads 0: it only measures the part lined up with itself.
level.2-4.tasks.2-4.bench.stages.1.note: Now the sin probe is on too, and the bench shows both readings: a from cos and b from sin. Which way of combining them equals the wave's amplitude, 0.30, however far it is shifted?
level.2-4.tasks.2-4.bench.stages.1.statu: Pick a combination and see what it gives at different angles.
level.2-4.tasks.2-4.bench.stages.1.title: Two probes
level.2-4.tasks.2-4.bench.stages.1.win: cos and sin each measure a part: a = A·cos φ and b = A·sin φ. √(a² + b²) is exactly A, however far the wave is shifted.
level.2-4.tasks.2-4.brief: The input is a wave of frequency 3 that can be shifted sideways, and the probe is frequency 3 too. First see whether the probe still measures it once shifted, then find a way of reading that does not mind the shift.
level.2-4.tasks.2-4.hint: The cos probe measures the part lined up with it. Shifted by a quarter of a cycle, how much is still lined up?
level.2-4.title: A shifted wave
level.2-5.after: This is the Fourier transform: multiply the signal per-pixel by the cos and the sin of each frequency, and average. Together the two readings a and b give the amplitude 2·√(a² + b²), however far the wave is shifted; how far it is shifted (the phase) is atan2(b, a). A probe with only cos measures a wave shifted by 90° as 0. Images work the same way, except that waves have two directions: run the probe once for every (kx, ky) and draw the amplitude it measures in cell (kx, ky), and you have the image's spectrum. The centre is (0, 0), the average brightness.
level.2-5.intro.0.t: <level-ref to="2-3"></level-ref> and <level-ref to="2-4"></level-ref> showed on the bench how a probe works. This level builds it as a circuit: the input is a curve of several waves mixed, some of them shifted, and you read off the amplitude of the frequency-3 wave.

level.2-6.after: Out of focus means blurred, and blurring turns the high frequencies down. So the brighter the outer part of the spectrum, the sharper the photo. A phone camera computes a score like this while it moves the lens, and stops where the score is highest.

level.2-6.intro.2.t: A new way of drawing, <part-ref to="spectrum"></part-ref>: how strong the wave at each frequency is, with frequency (0, 0) at the centre and higher frequencies further out.

level.2-7.after: A blur in space equals multiplying every frequency by a gain in the frequency domain: the convolution theorem. A sharp cut-off gain, turned back into space, is a kernel with negative side lobes, so rings appear beside edges (ringing); a gain that falls smoothly has hardly any. A Gaussian gain turned back into space is still a Gaussian, and that is the blur the expected output used.
level.2-7.intro.0.t: Stereos often have an "equaliser": a row of sliders, each in charge of a range of pitch, so you can push up the bass and pull down a harsh treble. Pictures can be treated the same way: give each frequency a volume, called a gain, where 1 keeps it as it is and 0 removes it entirely.
level.2-7.intro.1.t: The new part <part-ref to="part:fqApply"></part-ref>: takes a picture into the frequency domain, multiplies each frequency by the number in the matching cell of a gain picture, and comes back. The gain picture is laid out like a spectrum, with frequency (0, 0) at the centre.
level.2-7.intro.2.t: The 3×3 average and the Gaussian worked on the picture, mixing each pixel with its neighbours. This level works from the frequency side, and the result is a blur too. Something to think about: how are the two approaches related?

level.2-7.intro.3.t: Your task in this level: make a gain picture from "Frequency radius" so the output is as soft as the expected one, with no ripples.
level.2-7.tasks.2-7.brief: The expected output is a soft blur with no ripples at all. This time you do not blur on the picture; you go to the frequency domain instead: give each frequency a gain and process the photo with <part-ref to="part:fqApply"></part-ref>. You make the gain picture yourself, from "Frequency radius".

level.2-8.after: Just as in <level-ref to="2-7"></level-ref>: a hard disk cuts sharply, which is the same as a convolution with a kernel that has negative lobes, so rings of light and dark ripple out on both sides of an edge (ringing). A Gaussian mask falls off smoothly; its kernel is still a Gaussian, with no ripples. The expected image is in fact a spatial Gaussian blur with σ = 1, which matches a mask width of R = N/(2πσ) = 32/(2π) ≈ 5. Convolution in space equals multiplication in the frequency domain: this is the convolution theorem.

level.2-8.intro.0.t: Night shots on a phone and scans of old photos often have a layer of fine noise. The finer the grain, the faster it changes, and the farther from the centre it sits in the spectrum. Large shapes in the image change slowly and sit near the centre.
level.2-8.intro.1.t: What you built in <level-ref to="2-7"></level-ref> is now the <part-ref to="freq-filter"></part-ref> part: it keeps a disc of frequencies around the centre. level.3-1.after: Under frontal light, the normal’s z component measures how directly the surface faces the light: points facing it are brightest and tilted points are darker.
level.3-1.intro.0.t: Where does light and shade in a photograph come from? Start with a white matte surface lit from the camera direction. Its orientation affects how much light reaches each point.
level.3-1.intro.1.t: At each point, a unit normal points perpendicular to the surface and describes its orientation. Its three components follow the axes: x points right, y down, and z toward the camera. Their signs give direction along each axis, and their magnitudes show how much of the normal points along it. The three component images are given as inputs.
level.3-1.tasks.3-1.brief: The light shines from the front, in direction (0, 0, 1). Each point on the white surface has brightness equal to the cosine of the angle between its normal and the light direction. Draw the brightness image from the given normal components; you do not need to add any parts.
level.3-1.tasks.3-1.hidden.0.label: White ridge
level.3-1.tasks.3-1.hint: The light direction has only a z component. The cosine between two unit directions is the sum of their pairwise component products.
level.3-1.tasks.3-1.inputDescriptions.al: How much light the surface reflects. Here the entire surface is white, with reflectance 1, so the image is white throughout.
level.3-1.tasks.3-1.inputDescriptions.nx: The normal's left–right component. Opposite sides of the bump face opposite ways, so one side of the image is dark and the other light.
level.3-1.tasks.3-1.inputDescriptions.ny: The normal's up–down component. The upper and lower sides of the bump face opposite ways.
level.3-1.tasks.3-1.inputDescriptions.nz: The component of the normal toward the camera. The top of the bump and the flat plate face the camera and appear brighter in this image; the slopes appear darker.

level.3-10.after: Taking slopes removes an overall brightening (the offset); dividing by the steepest slope removes an overall scaling (the gain). When you design a feature, first ask: which changes should not change the answer? This is called invariance. Mind the padding outside the image: padding with 0 creates a fake edge at the border that changes with the lighting, so replicate the edge instead.
level.3-10.intro.0.t: Finding edges needs one more step: a threshold, so that only pixels whose gradient exceeds it count as edges. Too low, and fine texture counts too; too high, and real edges are missed.
level.3-10.intro.1.fig.caption: The same F with a dimmer lamp: the expected edges stay the same
level.3-10.intro.1.t: The trouble is lighting. A car's camera must recognise the same kerb at noon and at dusk; it cannot retune the threshold every time the light changes. The same face indoors and outdoors gives very different pixel values, yet the answer should be the same.
level.3-10.intro.2.t: New in this level is the part <part-ref to="part:globalMax"></part-ref>: it finds the largest number in its input and outputs a picture filled with that number everywhere.

level.3-12.after: One photo gives one brightness, which depends on both the paint and the facing, and the two cannot be told apart. Take another photo under another lamp: the paint is the same in both, so comparing them cancels it, and what is left depends only on the facing. This is photometric stereo: with a few known lamps, the facing of a surface is solved from its shading.
level.3-12.intro.0.t: Painted metal sheets on a line must be checked for dents and scratches. These change which way the surface faces, but the paint is uneven, so the shading in a single photo cannot tell paint from dent. The last three levels of this chapter build this inspection machine.

level.3-12.intro.1.t: Each sheet is photographed under three lamps: from the right, from below and from the front, with their directions in the brief. The paint is the same in all three photos; only the lamp changes.
level.3-12.intro.2.t: Your task in this level: mark where the surface leans to the right. Something to think about: what could make a spot dark in one photo? What relation between two photos has nothing to do with the paint?
level.3-12.tasks.3-12.brief: Metal sheets on the line are painted unevenly, some patches darker than others. Each sheet is photographed under three lamps: from the right (0.6, 0, 0.8), from below (0, 0.6, 0.8) and from the front (0, 0, 1). level.3-5.after: A whole spectrum, squeezed by three kinds of sensor into three numbers: that is the colour a camera (and an eye) sees.
level.3-5.intro.0.t: Each pixel of a colour photo has three numbers: R, G and B. But real light is not three kinds; it is a whole band like a rainbow, from violet to red, called a spectrum.
level.3-5.intro.1.fig.caption: Set 1: the daylight spectrum and the three sensitivity curves
level.3-5.intro.1.t: A camera, like the human eye, has only three kinds of sensor, each sensitive to a range of wavelengths. How sensitive each is at each wavelength, drawn out, is its sensitivity curve.
level.3-5.intro.2.t: This level's inputs are all waveforms: a spectrum and three sensitivity curves, 10 points each, from violet to red. <part-ref to="mean"></part-ref> turns a row of numbers into one number.
level.3-5.intro.3.t: Calculate the R, G and B readings and connect them to the matching output ports to see the resulting colour pixel. Unconnected colour channels are zero; connect the Image port to output a whole image directly.
level.3-5.tasks.3-5.brief: The "Spectrum" is how much light there is in each of 10 bands from violet (400 nm) to red (700 nm). The camera has three kinds of sensor, each with a sensitivity curve. Each sensor reads the spectrum times its sensitivity curve, averaged. Connect the three readings to the R, G and B output ports.

level.3-7.after: Brightness in a photograph depends on both surface colour and illumination. In this model, known illumination lets us recover RGB reflectance; where no light reaches the surface, the photo contains no colour information.
level.3-7.intro.0.t: So far you have looked at a single surface. In a real photo, a surface's own colour and the light falling on it are mixed together: a white wall in shadow looks grey, and dark floor tiles in sunlight can look very bright.
level.3-7.intro.1.t: Finding objects often relies on places where brightness jumps. Shadows make brightness jumps too. Something to think about: is a line between light and dark in a photo always the edge of an object? A phone app removing the shadow from a scanned page runs into exactly this.

level.3-7.tasks.3-7.brief: The brightness of each point in a photo = the surface's own colour (its reflectance) × the light reaching that point. The second input tells you how much light each point gets (1 is full light; in shadow it is much less). Remove the shadows and shading and output only the surface's own colour.

level.3-9.after: Combining the slopes in two directions into one length makes edge strength independent of edge direction: horizontal, vertical and diagonal edges are equally bright. The direction itself is atan2(gy, gx); the arrow always points where the brightness rises fastest, and on an edge it is perpendicular to the edge. Draw the input in the "Slope" view: the arrows are drawn at every pixel.
level.3-9.intro.0.t: So much for where light and shade come from. This level turns to edges: places where brightness changes fast. To find them, first say how fast the brightness changes at each point.
level.3-9.intro.1.fig.caption: Sobel x on a disc: strong on the left and right, almost nothing at the top and bottom
level.3-9.intro.1.t: A slope has two components: how much the brightness changes going right (gx), and going down (gy). Together they make an arrow called the gradient. Sobel x measures gx at every pixel, and Sobel y measures gy.
level.3-9.intro.2.t: The difficulty is direction. Object edges run horizontally, vertically and diagonally; measuring the slope in one direction only misses some of them. A good edge strength should not get weaker just because an edge turns.
level.3-9.intro.3.t: A new way of drawing, "Slope": contour lines, with an arrow at each place pointing where the picture brightens fastest.

level.3-9.tasks.3-9.brief: A slope has two components: Sobel x measures how much the brightness changes going right (gx), and Sobel y going down (gy). Together they make an arrow; at every pixel, output how long that arrow is: √(gx² + gy²). Whether an edge is horizontal, vertical or diagonal, the steeper it is, the brighter.

level.4-1.after: Training is walking downhill: think of the error (the mean of the squared differences) as a landscape, with w as where you stand. Each step moves down the slope by "learning rate × slope". Too small a learning rate takes many steps; too large overshoots the bottom and flies further away each time. A network has millions of knobs, and the principle is exactly the same.
level.4-1.intro.0.t: In earlier chapters you set every part's parameters by hand: how much blur, how high a threshold. But the models behind face recognition in your photo app or voice typing have thousands upon thousands of numbers, and nobody can turn them one by one. The machine has to tune itself.
level.4-1.intro.1.t: To tune itself, it first needs to know how badly tuned it is right now. That score is the error: how far the model's outputs are from the samples' correct answers, squared and averaged. The smaller the error, the better.
level.4-1.intro.2.t: The new part <part-ref to="part:lrnConst"></part-ref> is a number you do not fill in; multiply the input by it and you have w × input. When a circuit has learnable parts, <wiki-ref to="training"></wiki-ref> appears in the panel: at every step the machine feels which way the error slopes down and nudges the knob that way.

level.4-11.intro.0.t: So far every part's output has been as big as its input. In a real convolutional network the picture usually shrinks layer by layer: a photo has millions of pixels, and only after shrinking can the later layers keep up.
level.4-11.intro.1.t: A convolution layer's window is the familiar 3×3 kernel: it stops at one place, works out a number, then moves on. How far it moves each time is the stride.

level.4-16.after: A residual connection passes the input along a shortcut and lets the convolution branch learn an adjustment: y = x + F(x). When the target is close to the input, the network can start near the identity and learn the needed change. The shortcut also provides a direct path for gradients, but does not guarantee that every deep network will train successfully. The sharpening task here is simple and does not require every layer to learn a different feature.
level.4-16.intro.0.t: A deeper network can combine earlier results in later layers to see features over a wider area. But as layers accumulate, training can also become difficult.

level.4-18.after: Softmax turns scores into weights that sum to 1. Differences between scores determine the ratios of the weights; equal scores receive equal weights. The same method works for three or more scores.
level.4-18.intro.0.t: A classifier usually gives each possible class a score. Scores can be negative and do not necessarily sum to 1.
level.4-18.intro.1.t: Start with two classes: turn their scores into two nonnegative weights that sum to 1, so their relative support can be compared. Here we use the Softmax rule.
level.4-18.intro.2.t: Take the exponential of each score, then divide each result by their sum. Build this calculation first; afterwards the Softmax part becomes available.
level.4-18.tasks.4-18.brief: Given scores A and B, output their Softmax weights: P(A) = e^A ÷ (e^A + e^B), P(B) = e^B ÷ (e^A + e^B).
level.4-18.tasks.4-18.hint: Apply exp to each score, then add the results. The two weights share the same denominator.

level.4-19.after: The training error keeps falling, but the error on new samples (the validation set) falls and then rises: in the second half the model is memorising noise. This is called overfitting. One fix is early stopping: stop where the validation error is lowest. The other is regularisation: put a cost on large weights (L2), so the model will not bend the curve sharply just to hit a few points. Too small a λ cannot hold off overfitting; too large and the model cannot learn even the true rule (underfitting). When training real networks, part of the data is kept back for validation only, precisely so you can see this falls-then-rises line.
level.4-19.intro.0.t: Memorise past exam papers with their answers before a test and you get every old question right, but still cannot do the new ones. Models do this too: getting more and more accurate on the training samples does not mean being accurate on new samples.
level.4-19.intro.1.t: So you keep back some samples the model has never seen, just for checking. On the bench the filled dots are training samples and the hollow dots are new samples. Every sample carries a little random deviation (noise); the true pattern is a smooth curve.
level.4-19.intro.2.t: Here the new samples help choose when to stop and how much to regularise, so they act as a validation set. Real projects also keep a test set for evaluation after those choices are made. Repeatedly tuning against the test set makes the final score unreliable.
level.4-19.intro.3.t: Another kind of regularisation is dropout: during training, randomly switch off some neurons temporarily so the network does not rely too heavily on a fixed path. Validation and testing do not randomly switch them off. This bench demonstrates early stopping and L2, not dropout.
level.4-19.intro.4.t: Your task: decide at which step training should stop, then try another way of keeping the model in check. Something to think about: as the training error keeps shrinking, does the model keep getting better on new samples too?
level.4-19.tasks.4-19.bench.stages.0.not: The filled dots are the 10 training samples (with noise); the hollow dots are new samples the model has never been shown. Drag "Steps trained" and watch how the curve changes and how the two error lines below move. Stop at the step where the error on new samples is lowest.
level.4-19.tasks.4-19.bench.stages.1.not: This time training runs to the end, but the error gets an extra term: the larger the weights, the bigger the penalty (λ × the sum of all the squared weights). Tune λ to make the error on new samples as low as you can.

level.4-19.tasks.4-19.bench.win: The error on new samples is close to its minimum.
level.4-19.tasks.4-19.brief: The longer you train, the more accurate the model gets on the training samples. But what we want is for it to be accurate on new samples it has never seen as well. A flexible model trained too long memorises the noise in the samples too.
level.4-19.tasks.4-19.hint: Keep your eye on the two error lines: the training error keeps going down, while the error on new samples first falls, then rises. While it rises, what is the model learning?

level.4-20.after: Softmax turns scores into nonnegative weights that sum to 1 for any number of classes. The weights can be used as class probabilities, but their reliability still needs calibration and evaluation.
level.4-20.intro.0.t: The sorting machine needs to recognise X, O and + parts. From a camera image, the network first gives each class a score and then decides which kind it is.
level.4-20.intro.1.t: Choosing one of three, the network first gives each class a score. But scores can be positive or negative and do not add up to 1, so they cannot be read as "how sure" directly.
level.4-20.intro.2.t: Training a classifier also needs a measure of how wrong a prediction is. Cross-entropy, a common choice, looks at the probability assigned to the correct class: the lower that probability, the larger the loss. The game trainer uses squared error, a different loss.
level.4-20.intro.3.t: With many classes, we can check whether the top prediction is correct (top-1) or whether the correct class is among the top five (top-5). If the answer ranks second, top-1 counts it wrong and top-5 counts it right; they answer different questions.

level.4-20.tasks.4-20.brief: The sorting machine has to put parts into three classes: X, O and +. The network first gives each class a score: S1, S2 and S3 correspond to X, O and +. Scores may be positive or negative. Turn the three scores into three probabilities, each between 0 and 1, adding up to 1, with a higher score getting a higher probability. The expected output uses e^score ÷ the sum of the three e^score.

level.4-3.intro.2.t: Training first computes an output with the current parameters and compares it with the answer to obtain a loss. level.4-3.intro.3.t: Real training often divides samples into mini-batches: one batch contributes to an update; one pass through the training set is an epoch. Batch size and the number of epochs are training choices, not weights learned by the network.

level.4-5.after: A weighted sum and then a squash: that is a neuron. w1·diagonal + w2·curved + b = 0 is a straight line in the plane, and the neuron says "yes" on one side and "no" on the other: one neuron is one dividing line. The squash 1 / (1 + e^(−z)) is called the sigmoid.
level.4-5.intro.0.t: The name "neural network" comes from the brain: a nerve cell receives many signals and fires when together they are strong enough. A neuron in a computer is a simplified version, a computing unit that does one small thing.
level.4-5.intro.1.t: Each test is a letter picture already reduced to two numbers: how much diagonal stroke and how much curved stroke. So a picture is a point in the plane, and the neuron gives each point a score.

level.5-1.intro.0.t: Convolution processes a local region at a time; attention lets a patch combine information from other patches. First explore Q, K and V, then build an attention circuit, and finally train simplified transformations that produce Q, K and V.
level.5-1.intro.1.t: A query Q is compared with each key K to obtain weights, which combine the corresponding values V. First use patches directly to observe these three roles.
level.5-1.intro.2.t: Vision models usually generate Q, K and V from the same patch features using different learnable transformations. The final task trains a simplified example.
level.5-1.tasks.5-1-experiment.after: Q and K determine the weights for the information, while V supplies the content to combine. Next, build a circuit for this calculation using each of two patches as both a key and a value.

level.5-1.tasks.5-1-training.brief: Continue from the previous circuit and transform the patches with learnable scalars before attention. Use three learnable constants to produce Q, K and V: transform a into Q, use the same K transformation for a and b, and likewise share the V transformation. Train the parameters to match the targets.
level.5-1.tasks.5-1-training.hint: Multiply patches by learnable constants; connect the same K constant and the same V constant to both patches. Compute weights from Q and K, then combine V with those weights. Training updates the three constants against the test targets.
level.5-1.tasks.5-1.after: Attention first compares a query with keys, then combines values using the resulting weights. Next, continue from this circuit and add learnable parameters to produce Q, K and V.
level.5-1.tasks.5-1.brief: Use patch a as the query, with a and b each acting as a key and a value. Compute scores for a with a and a with b: score = 4 × average(a × corresponding patch). Apply Softmax to the two scores: weight = e^score ÷ the sum of both e^score. Output the weighted sum of patches a and b.

level.5-7.after: When only positive pairs are pulled together, putting every image at the same point minimises the loss but tells nothing apart: this is called collapse. InfoNCE's denominator treats the other views in the batch as negative pairs and pushes them away, so the dots spread out round the circle. The alterations themselves supply the answer, with no human labels: this is self-supervised contrastive learning (SimCLR).
level.5-7.intro.0.t: Training in earlier chapters relied on labels: every image came with an answer written by a person. But in the real world almost no photos have labels, and labelling millions of images one by one is slow and expensive. Can a model still learn without answers?
level.5-7.intro.1.t: One way: make two altered versions of an image, shifted a little, brighter or darker, with some noise added. The two versions are certain to come from the same image, and that fact alone can serve as the answer. Many image models are first trained like this on huge numbers of unlabelled images.
level.5-7.intro.2.t: The encoder on the bench turns each view into a direction, drawn as a point on a circle; the two views of the same image are joined by a line and called a pair of partners. In the quiz, each view has to pick out its own partner from all the points.
level.5-7.intro.3.t: The loss has two terms: one pulls partners together, the other pushes away the other views in the same batch, and the second can be switched on or off. In this level you train the encoder. Before you start, think: with a good encoder, what should the points on the circle look like?

level.6-1.after: Harris corner detection combines gradients and their correlation in a neighbourhood to distinguish corners, straight edges and flat areas. The threshold selects strong responses; next we locate a point within each response region.
level.6-1.intro.0.t: To stitch overlapping photographs, we need corresponding positions in both images. Points in flat areas or along straight edges are easily confused with nearby positions; corners change in several directions and are often easier to find again.
level.6-1.intro.1.t: First use Sobel and a 3×3 average to observe local change. Straight edges also change strongly, so distinguishing corners requires considering how the two directions change together.
level.6-1.intro.2.t: The Harris method measures these changes with three local statistics and calculates a response. Continue the circuit through each step, then use a threshold to mark corners.
level.6-1.tasks.6-1-energy.after: Local change can be strong at both edges and corners, so it cannot distinguish them alone. Next, the Harris response accounts for the relationship between the two directions.
level.6-1.tasks.6-1-energy.brief: Calculate horizontal and vertical gradients, square each, average each over 3×3, and add them. Compare the results at straight edges and corners.
level.6-1.tasks.6-1-energy.hint: Use Sobel x and Sobel y for Gx and Gy. Multiply each image by itself, take a 3×3 average, then add the two results.

level.6-1.tasks.6-1-response.after: The Harris response combines change in both directions and their correlation: corners tend to have a strong positive response, straight edges a negative one, and flat areas a response near zero. Finally use a threshold to mark corners.
level.6-1.tasks.6-1-response.brief: Continue the circuit to calculate the Harris response. A and B are the 3×3 averages of Gx² and Gy²; C is the 3×3 average of Gx·Gy. C measures how the directions vary together: a diagonal edge can make A and B large, but C² offsets that case. Output 100 × [AB − C² − 0.05(A + B)²], and compare edges and corners.
level.6-1.tasks.6-1-response.hint: The previous circuit already has A, B and A+B. Multiply Gx and Gy and average over 3×3 for C; calculate AB−C² and 0.05×(A+B)², subtract, then multiply by 100. The 0.05 controls the penalty for edges; 100 only scales the response.
level.6-1.tasks.6-1.brief: Continue the Harris response circuit: output 1 where the response exceeds 0.22 and 0 elsewhere.

level.6-11.after: The homography H has 8 degrees of freedom and each pair of points gives 2 equations, so it needs at least 4 pairs; the game solved H from your pairs with DLT. Three pairs only fix an affine map (6 degrees of freedom), which keeps lines parallel and cannot fit a book seen in perspective. In a real pipeline the pairs come from candidates that passed the ratio test, and RANSAC picks them by repeatedly drawing 4 pairs and counting inliers.
level.6-11.intro.0.t: Point your phone at a book and an app can tell which book it is and even paste the cover image back into the photo; augmented reality (AR) often works like this. The hard part is that the book is shot at an angle, so in the photo it is no longer a neat rectangle.
level.6-11.intro.1.t: Pasting the cover back into the photo needs a transformation: it tells each point on the cover where it lands in the photo. The transformation is computed from a few pairs of corresponding points; choose the pairs well and the cover lands accurately.
level.6-11.intro.2.t: On the bench the cover is on the left and the photo on the right. Connect a point on the cover to the same point in the photo; the game computes the transformation from your point pairs, pastes the cover on and shows the average error.
level.6-11.intro.3.t: In this level you must paste the cover accurately, with an average error under 1.5 pixels. Before you start, look at the shape of the book in the photo: compared with the cover's original rectangle, what has changed?

level.6-4.after: In repeated texture the first and second places are almost equally close: however alike, such a match cannot be trusted. The ratio test d₁ / d₂ < 0.8 accepts only a match whose first place is clearly ahead, and an overall brightening does not change the ratio.
level.6-4.intro.0.t: Each image has some points that are easy to recognise, and they still have to be paired up: which point in the right image is this point from the left image? The most direct way is to compare how they look: take a small patch around it and search the right image for the most similar patch.
level.6-4.intro.1.t: Similarity is measured by a distance d: subtract the two patches pixel by pixel, square, add up, then take the square root. The smaller d is, the more alike they are. For each point, the closest match in the right image is first place, at distance d₁; the next is second place, at distance d₂.
level.6-4.intro.2.t: This level hands you the comparisons directly: each cell is a keypoint, and the three maps are its distances to three candidates. The nearest is not always to be trusted: if the second nearest is almost as near, the pair may be a mistake caused by repeated texture.

level.6-5.after: Subtract each window's own mean brightness first, and an overall brightening no longer affects the distance; divide by its own standard deviation as well, and even a contrast change does not matter. This is the idea behind normalised cross-correlation (NCC), and SIFT descriptors are normalised in a similar way.

level.6-6.after: The chance that both points of a round are inliers is p², and the chance that all k rounds miss is (1 − p²)ᵏ. To reach a success rate P you need k ≥ log(1 − P) / log(1 − pⁿ): with p = 0.5, n = 2 and P = 0.99 that is 17 rounds, and with only 30% inliers it takes 49. The number of rounds is set by the inlier ratio and δ by the noise; neither can stand in for the other.
level.6-6.intro.0.t: When matching points or finding lines, wrong points always creep in; these are called outliers, and the right ones inliers. If you fit one line to all the points, a few far-off outliers can drag it askew. Panorama stitching and lane detection both have to deal with them first.
level.6-6.intro.1.fig.caption: RANSAC pegboard: each round draws two pegs, and the pegs between the rails vote
level.6-6.intro.1.t: RANSAC takes a different approach: pick two points at random and join them with a line, then count how many points lie close enough to it to count as support. Repeat for many rounds and keep the line with the most support.
level.6-6.intro.2.t: On the bench you set two numbers: the number of rounds k, and δ, how close to the line a point must be to count as support. Each setting is run for 200 trials to see how often it finds the right line. There are three outlier ratios, and each has a cap on the number of rounds.
level.6-6.intro.3.t: In this level you choose a k for each of the three outlier ratios, plus one shared δ, so that every success rate reaches 99%. The questions are: as outliers increase, how should the number of rounds change? And what should decide δ?

level.6-6.tasks.6-6.brief: Each round draws 2 random points, joins them into a line and counts the points closer than δ to it; after k rounds the line with the most support is kept. For each of the three outlier ratios, use a k within the budget so that the success rate over 200 trials is ≥ 99%.
level.6-6.tasks.6-6.hint: The more outliers, the smaller the chance that a round draws two inliers. δ depends only on the noise: too small misses true inliers, too large counts outliers in as well.
level.6-6.title: Consensus
level.6-7.after: Least squares gets pulled a little by every speck; RANSAC trusts only the line with the most support and refits it on its inliers, so however many specks there are they cannot drag it. level.6-8.after: A SIFT descriptor divides the area round a keypoint into 4×4 small cells and makes an 8-direction histogram in each, 128 numbers in all. Directions follow the gradient and the magnitude is the vote: whichever way an edge brightens, the cell votes that way.
level.6-8.intro.0.t: Knowing where a point is is not enough to recognise it; you also need to record what its surroundings look like. SIFT does it by counting which way the edges around it face.

level.6-8.tasks.6-8.brief: Give each cell's gradient magnitude to the direction it is closest to: when the across part is larger, brightening to the right counts as "→" and to the left as "←"; when the down part is larger, brightening downwards counts as "↓" and upwards as "↑". The four outputs are the magnitude summed per direction, divided by the number of cells.

level.6-9.after: Hough turns "find a line" into "find a peak in the accumulator". With bins too fine, noise splits one line's votes into many small peaks; too coarse, and two nearby lines merge into one peak. The right bin size depends on the noise and on how far apart the lines are.
level.6-9.intro.0.t: Often what you are looking for is a line: a lane marking, the edge of a sheet of paper, the outline of a building. Edge detection only gives a scatter of loose points, mixed with noise and unrelated points. How do you pick out straight lines from that?
level.6-9.intro.1.t: The Hough transform lets the points vote. A straight line can be written down with two numbers: its direction θ and its distance ρ from the centre. Every point votes for all the lines passing through it, and a line that is really there collects lots of votes.
level.6-9.intro.2.t: Votes can only be counted once they land in cells: the (θ, ρ) plane is cut into a grid, which is called binning. These cells are on the right of the bench; the darker the colour, the more votes, and the marked 1 and 2 are the two peaks with the most votes.
level.6-9.intro.3.t: In this level you tune the bin size so that, in all three sets, the two peaks with the most votes are exactly the two lines. Before you start, think: how does the cell size affect the way votes gather together?

level.7-1.after: The shape only appears through matching: each image on its own is just speckle. Corresponding points only need to be searched for along the same row, and the larger the disparity, the nearer the object.
level.7-1.intro.0.t: Hold a finger up in front of your eyes and close your left and right eye in turn: which jumps more, your finger or the far wall? The distance by which the same thing is offset between your two eyes is called disparity.
level.7-1.intro.1.t: The stereo cameras on robots and cars also use disparity to judge distance. Both images in this level are random dots, and neither shows any shape on its own; in 1960 the psychologist Julesz used images like these to show that people can see depth without recognising any object.
level.7-1.intro.2.t: The new primitive <part-ref to="part:argmin4"></part-ref> takes four pictures and, cell by cell, outputs the number 0–3 of the one that is smallest.

level.7-1.intro.3.t: The output is a disparity map: each pixel holds 0 to 3, the number of pixels by which the thing there is offset between the two images. A few wrong pixels are fine. The question is: how can you tell that a pixel in the right image is the same spot as this pixel in the left image?

level.7-2.after: No window is best for every image: a large window resists noise but wipes out detail; a small one keeps detail but is vulnerable to noise. Many vision problems involve this kind of trade-off.

level.7-2.intro.1.t: Real stereo cameras have to pick this size too. A street scene has large stretches of wall, but also thin power poles and railings; in dim light the photos are full of noise. The same camera has to cope with all of it.

level.8-4.after: You cannot differentiate through the sampling step: with a fresh draw each time, training cannot tell whether a better result came from changing μ and σ or from luck. Write it as z = μ + σ·ε instead: all the randomness comes from the input ε, z is just a multiply and an add of μ and σ, and the gradient is perfectly clear. This is called reparameterization, and it is how a VAE's encoder is trained.
level.8-4.intro.0.t: The decoder from <level-ref to="8-1"></level-ref> can turn two numbers into a blob. If those two numbers are drawn at random, it can draw blobs it has never seen: that is generation. Random does not mean anything goes: the numbers are drawn from a normal distribution, so most land near the centre μ, and the larger σ is, the more they spread out.
level.8-4.intro.1.t: Training means nudging the parameters a little, seeing whether the result gets better or worse, and adjusting in the better direction; working out which way to nudge is called differentiating. level.8-6.after: If the judge stands still while the generator trains hard, the generator puts every sample on the one spot the judge trusts most: the two pens merge and draw only one cluster. This is mode collapse; as soon as the judge reacts, they jump together to the other cluster. Let the judge keep up and the generator take small steps, and the pens settle on one cluster each, until the judge's accuracy is back to 50%.
level.8-6.intro.0.t: Earlier, reconstruction error trained the encoder and decoder. Adversarial training uses a different signal: a discriminator tries to tell real and generated samples apart, and the generator improves its output using that judgement.
level.8-6.intro.1.t: Another way to generate is to have two models spar: a generator draws fake samples and a judge decides which are real. The better the judge gets at telling, the more convincing the generator has to be. This is called a generative adversarial network (GAN), and the "faces of people who don't exist" you see online are drawn this way.
level.8-6.intro.2.t: The real data on the bench is two clusters of points. The generator has two pens, each drawing in one spot. The judge is a curve D(x): the higher it is, the more the judge believes a point there is real.
level.8-6.intro.3.t: The two sides train in turns. You decide how many steps the judge trains each round, how many the generator trains, and how far the generator moves with each step.
level.8-6.intro.4.t: In this level both clusters must be drawn, leaving the judge only able to guess, with its accuracy back at one half. Before you start, think: what difference does it make which side trains more, and which moves faster?

level.8-9.after: Give the generator one more input, a condition, and it draws what is asked for: this is called conditional generation. Text prompts like "draw a cat" or "in watercolour" are just more elaborate conditions.
level.8-9.intro.0.t: What a generator draws is random. To make it draw what is asked for, it has to be told something more.
level.8-9.intro.1.fig.caption: Set 1: left
level.8-9.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: when c = 0, draw the blob in the region on the left; when c = 1, on the right.
level.8-9.tasks.8-9.brief: When c = 0, draw a blob from the region on the left; when c = 1, from the region on the right.
level.8-9.tasks.8-9.hidden.0.label: Left again
level.8-9.tasks.8-9.hint: The same sampling, only with a different centre. Can the centre be worked out from c?
level.8-9.tasks.8-9.tests.0.label: Left
level.8-9.tasks.8-9.tests.1.label: Right
level.8-9.tasks.8-9.tests.2.label: Right again
level.8-9.title: Draw it on the side asked for
level.9-1.after: A binary mask has the same size as the image, and each 0 or 1 records a class. It retains the foreground shape and location. If foreground and background intensities overlap, one threshold will mislabel pixels.
level.9-1.intro.0.t: Segmentation assigns a label to every pixel. Here we do binary segmentation: bright cells are foreground and the dark field is background. Before wiring, find the column between the two bright regions that should be background.
level.9-1.tasks.binary-foreground-mask.b: Label pixels strictly brighter than 0.5 as 1 and the rest as 0. Compare the examples with and without a narrow gap.
level.9-1.title: One label per pixel
level.9-10.after: An adaptive boundary, a coarse path that removes grain, a skip connection that keeps detail: a small U-Net-style pipeline. Real cell-segmentation networks replace every step with learnt convolutions, but the structure stays the same.
level.9-10.intro.0.t: A batch of slides comes from different microscopes and stains: some dark overall, some bright.
level.9-10.intro.1.fig.caption: Set 2: a bright slide
level.9-10.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: mark the cells on every slide, keeping the gaps.
level.9-10.tasks.9-10.brief: A batch of microscope slides, each with its own brightness and contrast, with cells touching. Mark the cells, and keep the gaps between them.
level.9-10.tasks.9-10.hidden.0.label: Low contrast
level.9-10.tasks.9-10.hint: A fixed threshold cannot be right on both dark slides and bright ones.
level.9-10.tasks.9-10.tests.0.label: A dark slide
level.9-10.tasks.9-10.tests.1.label: A bright slide
level.9-10.tasks.9-10.tests.2.label: A row of cells
level.9-10.title: Segmenting cells
level.9-2.after: Split into two, find each centre, split again: that is one step of k-means. Repeat a few steps and the boundary settles between the two heaps of pixels.
level.9-2.intro.0.t: When nobody tells the machine what is foreground and what is background, can it split the pixels into heaps by itself?
level.9-2.intro.1.t: One way: draw a boundary in brightness anywhere, split the pixels into two classes by it, look at each class's average, then move the boundary.
level.9-2.intro.2.fig.caption: Set 1: a round patch
level.9-2.intro.2.t: Your task in this level: by the rule in the brief, work out the new boundary after one move.
level.9-2.tasks.9-2.brief: Split the pixels into two classes by brightness: those brighter than the boundary m, and the rest. Work out each class's average brightness and output the new boundary halfway between them.
level.9-2.tasks.9-2.hidden.0.label: Round patch, split low
level.9-2.tasks.9-2.hint: A class's average = the sum of its pixels' brightness ÷ the number of its pixels. <part-ref to="mean"></part-ref> divides by the number of all the pixels, which cancels when one average is divided by another.
level.9-2.tasks.9-2.tests.0.label: A round patch
level.9-2.tasks.9-2.tests.1.label: A strip on the right
level.9-2.tasks.9-2.tests.2.label: Slanted stripes
level.9-2.title: Into classes
level.9-3.after: Without being told what the foreground is, k-means splits the pixels into two heaps by itself. But it looks only at brightness: two things of the same brightness, it cannot tell apart.
level.9-3.intro.0.t: The <part-ref to="kmeansStep"></part-ref> in the tray splits the values into two classes at the boundary m and outputs halfway between the two class averages.
level.9-3.intro.1.fig.caption: Set 2: a strip on the right
level.9-3.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: take three steps from the starting boundary, then split every pixel into two classes.
level.9-3.tasks.9-3.brief: Starting from the given boundary, take three k-means steps, then split every pixel into two classes by the final boundary: output 1 for the bright class.
level.9-3.tasks.9-3.hidden.0.label: A darker round patch
level.9-3.tasks.9-3.hint: The starting boundary may be a long way off.
level.9-3.tasks.9-3.tests.0.label: A round patch
level.9-3.tasks.9-3.tests.1.label: A strip on the right
level.9-3.tasks.9-3.tests.2.label: Slanted stripes
level.9-3.title: Segmenting by brightness
level.9-4.after: Zero-upsample first, then run a kernel over it: that is a transposed convolution with stride 2, and the kernel decides which neighbours, in what proportion, fill the empty cells. The decoder of a segmentation network uses it to enlarge small feature maps layer by layer back to the size of the picture.
level.9-4.intro.0.t: The networks of earlier chapters make the picture smaller and smaller: pooling and downsampling shrink 16×16 to a few numbers that answer "what is this?". But to ask "what is every pixel?", the answer has to be as big as the original.
level.9-4.intro.1.fig.caption: A bright dot, zero-upsampled
level.9-4.intro.1.t: The new primitive <part-ref to="part:zeroUp"></part-ref> doubles the size: each pixel goes in the top left of a 2×2 block, and the other three cells are 0.
level.9-4.intro.2.fig.caption: Set 1: square
level.9-4.intro.2.t: Your task in this level: enlarge an 8×8 picture to 16×16, every pixel becoming a 2×2 block of the same value.
level.9-4.tasks.9-4.brief: Enlarge an 8×8 picture to 16×16: every pixel becomes a 2×2 block, all four cells the same.
level.9-4.tasks.9-4.hidden.0.label: One bright dot
level.9-4.tasks.9-4.hint: <part-ref to="part:zeroUp"></part-ref> puts each pixel in the top left of its 2×2. Where do the other three cells get their number?
level.9-4.tasks.9-4.tests.0.label: Square
level.9-4.tasks.9-4.tests.1.label: Diagonal
level.9-4.tasks.9-4.tests.2.label: Ramp
level.9-4.title: Twice the size
level.9-5.after: Change the kernel and the same transposed convolution goes from "copy one cell to four" to smooth enlargement. In a network this kernel is learnt: the decoder learns for itself how best to enlarge.
level.9-5.intro.0.t: The Transposed convolution in the tray zero-upsamples to twice the size, then runs a 3×3 kernel over it; you fill in the kernel yourself.
level.9-5.intro.1.fig.caption: Ramp
level.9-5.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: enlarge more smoothly; the rule is in the brief.
level.9-5.tasks.9-5.brief: Twice the size again, this time smoothly: the original pixels stay as they are, an empty cell takes the average of the two original pixels on either side (or above and below), and a corner cell the average of four.
level.9-5.tasks.9-5.hidden.0.label: One bright dot
level.9-5.tasks.9-5.hint: Which surrounding cells does one original pixel go to, and how much to each?
level.9-5.tasks.9-5.tests.0.label: Square
level.9-5.tasks.9-5.tests.1.label: Diagonal
level.9-5.tasks.9-5.tests.2.label: Ramp
level.9-5.title: Bilinear enlargement
level.9-6.after: This is max unpooling: the encoder remembers where each maximum was when pooling, and the decoder puts it back there when enlarging, so details are not smeared over the whole block. SegNet works like this.
level.9-6.intro.0.t: Max pooling keeps the largest number of each 2×2 block, but does not record which cell of the block it was in. When enlarging back, where should it go?
level.9-6.intro.1.fig.caption: First set
level.9-6.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: put each pooled value back in the cell it came from, with the rest of the block 0. The picture before pooling is given too.
level.9-6.tasks.9-6.brief: Each 2×2 block's largest value was pooled into one cell. Put it back in the cell of the block it came from, with the other three cells of the block 0.
level.9-6.tasks.9-6.hidden.0.label: Set 4
level.9-6.tasks.9-6.hint: First enlarge the small picture to block size; which cell of the block equals the enlarged value?
level.9-6.tasks.9-6.tests.0.label: Set 1
level.9-6.tasks.9-6.tests.1.label: Set 2
level.9-6.tasks.9-6.tests.2.label: Set 3
level.9-6.title: Back where it came from
level.9-7.after: Pooling throws part of the position away, and unpooling gets it back: which cell of the 2×2 block the dot was in is still in the picture before pooling.
level.9-7.intro.0.t: The <part-ref to="unpool"></part-ref> in the tray puts each pooled value back in the cell it came from before pooling; every other cell is 0.
level.9-7.intro.1.fig.caption: Set 1: three dots
level.9-7.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: pool a picture of bright dots and enlarge it back, with every dot returning to its place.
level.9-7.tasks.9-7.brief: A picture of sparse bright dots goes through 2×2 max pooling, then back up to 16×16, and every dot must return to where it was.
level.9-7.tasks.9-7.hidden.0.label: Four dots
level.9-7.tasks.9-7.hint: Enlarge it and every dot smears into a whole block.
level.9-7.tasks.9-7.tests.0.label: Three dots
level.9-7.tasks.9-7.tests.1.label: Dots side by side
level.9-7.tasks.9-7.tests.2.label: Dots at the edge
level.9-7.title: Pool and back again
level.9-8.after: Shrinking averages several cells so the grain cancels out; decide, then enlarge back: this is an encoder–decoder. The price is that boundaries can only line up with the blocks: anything finer than a block is lost in the shrinking.
level.9-8.intro.0.t: To count and measure cells under a microscope, the first step is marking whether every pixel is a cell. But the slide is full of grain.
level.9-8.intro.1.fig.caption: Set 1: two cells
level.9-8.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: mark the cells (1) and the background (0).
level.9-8.tasks.9-8.brief: Cells under a microscope, with heavy grain. Mark the cells (1) and the background (0).
level.9-8.tasks.9-8.hidden.0.label: One big, one small
level.9-8.tasks.9-8.hint: Looked at cell by cell, the grain fools the threshold. What about several cells at once?
level.9-8.tasks.9-8.tests.0.label: Two cells
level.9-8.tasks.9-8.tests.1.label: A long cell
level.9-8.tasks.9-8.tests.2.label: Three cells
level.9-8.title: Shrink, then enlarge
level.9-9.after: Combine the coarse result enlarged back with the fine result at full size: the coarse path keeps out the grain, the fine path keeps the detail. This line straight from encoder to decoder is called a skip connection, and U-Net has one at every level.
level.9-9.intro.0.t: Cells often crowd together with only a very thin gap between them. When counting, lose the gap and two count as one.
level.9-9.intro.1.fig.caption: Set 1: two touching
level.9-9.intro.1.t: Your task in this level: mark the cells, keeping the gaps between them.
level.9-9.tasks.9-9.brief: Touching cells are separated only by a dark gap one pixel wide. Mark the cells, and keep the gaps (0).
level.9-9.tasks.9-9.hidden.0.label: Two in a row, gap elsewhere
level.9-9.tasks.9-9.hint: The shrink-then-enlarge path cannot see a one-pixel gap. The original picture still can.
level.9-9.tasks.9-9.tests.0.label: Two touching
level.9-9.tasks.9-9.tests.1.label: One above the other
level.9-9.tasks.9-9.tests.2.label: Three in a row
level.9-9.title: The thin line is gone
piece.add.desc: Adds two pictures pixel by pixel: a + b
piece.add.name: Add
piece.addNoise.desc: Outputs √ᾱ·x₀ + √(1 − ᾱ)·ε: x₀ noised straight to step t.
piece.addNoise.name: Add noise
piece.apMeter.desc: Reads right or wrong in score order, the ranks and the number labelled G, and outputs the AP.
piece.apMeter.name: AP meter
piece.argmin4.desc: Compares cost maps pixel by pixel and outputs the index of the smallest
piece.argmin4.name: Index of minimum
piece.arith.desc: Adds, subtracts, multiplies or divides two pictures pixel by pixel. Either side can be set to a constant; the other receives a wire
piece.arith.name: Arithmetic
piece.attention.desc: Cuts the image into P×P patches; each patch takes the average of every patch's v, weighted by softmax(q·k/√d). With only Q wired, K and V use it too
piece.attention.name: Attention
piece.blur3h.desc: Each cell becomes the average of itself and its left and right neighbours
piece.blur3h.name: 3-point horizontal average
piece.box3.desc: Each cell becomes the average of the nine cells in the 3×3 block around it
piece.box3.name: 3×3 average
piece.const.desc: Always outputs the same number. Added to or multiplied with a picture, it applies to every cell
piece.const.name: Constant
piece.cross.desc: Outputs the cross product a × b of two 3-vectors.
piece.cross.name: Cross product
piece.dg_decode.desc: Draws an image back from those numbers (weights come from training)
piece.dg_decode.name: Decoder
piece.dg_decoder.desc: Two numbers → one blob: z₁ moves it left–right, z₂ up–down
piece.dg_decoder.name: Decoder (trained)
piece.dg_encode.desc: Squeezes the whole image into a row of k numbers (weights come from training)
piece.dg_encode.name: Encoder
piece.dg_encoder.desc: One blob → two numbers: where it is left–right and up–down
piece.dg_encoder.name: Encoder (trained)
piece.dg_mu.desc: Two trainable numbers: the centre of the distribution
piece.dg_reparam.desc: Randomness enters only through ε; μ and σ differentiate as usual
piece.dg_reparam.name: Reparameterization μ + σ·ε
piece.dg_sample.desc: Draws a fresh random number every time it runs
piece.dg_sample.name: Sample z ~ N(μ, σ²)
piece.dg_sigma.desc: Two trainable numbers: how spread out the distribution is
piece.diffx.name: Horizontal difference
piece.disparity.desc: Matches the left and right images row by row and outputs disparity; window size selectable
piece.disparity.inputs.0.label: left
piece.disparity.inputs.1.label: right
piece.disparity.name: Disparity search
piece.downsample.desc: Keeps every other pixel, halving the size
piece.downsample.name: Downsample
piece.embed.desc: Turns a picture into 4×4 = 16 features of length 1: brightening, a contrast change, a shift of a pixel or two or a little noise hardly move it
piece.embed.name: Contrastive encoder
piece.epiline.desc: Reads the three columns of F and a point (x, y), and outputs the epipolar line F·p.
piece.epiline.name: Epipolar line
piece.fqApply.desc: Takes the picture into the frequency domain, multiplies each frequency by the number in the matching cell of the gain picture, and comes back. The gain picture is laid out like a spectrum: its centre is frequency (0, 0)
piece.fqApply.name: Multiply in frequency
piece.fqLowpass.desc: Transforms to the frequency domain, multiplies by a mask centred on the middle, and transforms back
piece.fqLowpass.name: Frequency low-pass
piece.fqMean.desc: Averages a row of numbers into a single number
piece.fqMean.name: Compute the average
piece.fqSpectrum.desc: The centred, log-scaled magnitude spectrum: the centre is the average brightness, and further out means faster change
piece.fqSpectrum.name: Frequency spectrum
piece.fqWave.desc: A wave of 32 points: cos or sin(2π·k·x/32), swinging between −1 and 1
piece.fqWave.name: Wave
piece.gauss.name: Gaussian blur
piece.globalMax.desc: Fills every cell with the maximum of the picture
piece.globalMax.name: Global max
piece.gradmag.name: Magnitude of the gradient
piece.harris.desc: Harris corner response: large and positive where the picture changes in both directions, negative along straight edges
piece.harris.name: Harris response
piece.homography.desc: Pairs come four numbers at a time: (x, y) → (x′, y′). With k = 0 it solves from all the pairs (DLT); with k > 0 it runs RANSAC: k rounds each solve H from 4 random pairs and count the pairs it maps within 1.5 pixels, and the largest group is solved again. Outputs the 9 numbers of H
piece.homography.name: Solve homography
piece.hough.desc: Every point brighter than 0.5 votes for each line x·cosθ + y·sinθ = ρ through it: across is θ (16 cells, 0° … 180°), down is ρ (2 pixels a cell)
piece.hough.name: Hough accumulator
piece.invert.desc: Every pixel becomes 1 − itself: light turns dark and dark turns light
piece.invert.name: Invert
piece.iou.desc: Outputs the intersection over union of two box masks: the overlap divided by the area they cover together.
piece.iou.name: IoU
piece.kernel3.name: 3×3 kernel
piece.kmeansStep.desc: Splits the values into two classes at the boundary m and outputs halfway between the two class averages.
piece.kmeansStep.name: One k-means step
piece.learn3.desc: 3×3 kernel whose weights are set by training
piece.learn3.name: Learnable 3×3 kernel
piece.lrnConst.desc: A number that training sets. Added to or multiplied with a picture, it applies to every cell
piece.lrnConst.name: Learnable constant
piece.lrnConv.desc: Learnable 3×3 kernel, starting from a set of very small random numbers
piece.lrnConv.name: Conv layer
piece.lrnDense.desc: Learnable weight w and bias b
piece.lrnDense.name: Dense w·x + b
piece.lrnRes.name: Residual block
piece.lrnRgb.desc: One kernel spans R, G and B: 3×3×3 learnable weights
piece.lrnRgb.name: Multichannel 3×3 kernel
piece.matcher.desc: Outputs the number 1–3 of the nearest when its distance is under 0.8 times the second nearest; otherwise 0.
piece.matcher.name: Matcher
piece.max.desc: Takes the larger of two pictures, cell by cell
piece.max.name: The larger one
piece.maxpool.desc: Takes the maximum of each 2×2 block, halving the size
piece.maxpool.name: 2×2 max pool
piece.merge.desc: Has three inputs and adds the pictures wired into them pixel by pixel; an empty input is skipped
piece.merge.name: Merger
piece.mul.desc: Multiplies two pictures pixel by pixel: a × b
piece.mul.name: Multiply
piece.occlusion.desc: Covers the 3×3 round every cell with a grey (0.5) block and outputs how far the classifier's score drops. The photo goes into in, the weights into w.
piece.occlusion.name: Occlusion map
piece.peaks.desc: Outputs 1 where a cell is no smaller than its 3×3 neighbours and above 0.3, and 0 elsewhere.
piece.peaks.name: Peak finder
piece.ransac.desc: Among the points brighter than 0.5, k rounds each join two random points and count the points closer than δ; the best line is refitted on its inliers and drawn (cells closer than 0.7 are 1)
piece.ransac.name: RANSAC line
piece.restore.desc: Outputs (x_t − √(1 − ᾱ)·ε) / √ᾱ: x₀ recovered from x_t and the noise ε.
piece.restore.name: Restore
piece.sense.desc: What one kind of sensor reads from a spectrum: the spectrum times its sensitivity curve, averaged
piece.sense.name: Sensor
piece.shade.desc: Reflectance × (normal · lamp direction), 0 where the surface faces away
piece.shade.name: Lambert shading
piece.shift.desc: Shifts the whole picture by one pixel; cells shifted in from the border are 0
piece.shift.name: Shift
piece.softmax.desc: Turns two or three scores into weights that sum to 1. Leave the third input empty for two scores; its output is then 0.
piece.sqrt.name: Square root
piece.sub.desc: Subtracts two pictures pixel by pixel: a − b
piece.sub.name: Subtract
piece.tconv.desc: Zero-upsamples to twice the size, then runs a 3×3 kernel over it
piece.tconv.name: Transposed convolution (stride 2)
piece.threshold.name: Threshold
piece.unpool.desc: Puts each pooled value back in the cell it came from before pooling; every other cell is 0.
piece.unpool.name: Unpool
piece.warp.desc: Carries the picture by H onto a picture the size of the "canvas": each cell of the canvas takes the cell of the picture that H⁻¹ points to (the nearest one), and 0 where that falls outside
piece.warp.name: Homography warp
piece.zeroUp.desc: Doubles the size: each pixel goes in the top left of a 2×2 block, the other three are 0
piece.zeroUp.name: Zero upsample
